title: 28 · Moving forward
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 28 · Moving forward
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Name the parts of a research project that stay with you when tools do the coding and the labelling.
Say what a given measurement instrument cannot see, and write that limit into a methods section.
Name the independent source you would compare a variable in your own research with, and what that comparison would show a referee.
List what you read recently outside economics, and what each piece made you want to measure.
Lay out how you would learn a new method on your own.

title: 28 · Moving forward
text:
What we cover

Many advances in economics came from measuring something nobody had measured before. Two survey articles, papers that summarise a field’s methods and findings for people new to it, trace this for economic activity seen from space and for sentiment read from text:

Donaldson & Storeygard (JEP, 2016) on how economists use satellite data, from the science of remote sensing to open questions.
Gentzkow, Kelly & Taddy (JEL, 2019) on how economists turn digital text into variables, and the statistical methods involved.

What the tools do not replace. A model will answer a badly posed question, and a pipeline will run on a variable that means nothing. Choosing the question and judging whether the variable measures what you claim stay with you, and they decide the quality of the work.
Know what your instrument cannot see. A measurement instrument (the device or data source that records a quantity, such as a satellite sensor or a survey) sees part of what you care about, so the variable you build from it is often a proxy, an observable stand-in for something you cannot observe, such as lights for income. A vegetation index tracks greenness, which is only partly yield. Transcripts drop what the room knew. A classifier’s label is a prediction with an error rate (the share of cases it labels wrongly, measured on examples whose answers are known), and it belongs in the analysis as one. Measurement error, the gap between the recorded and the true value, has a cost: random errors in an explanatory variable shrink its estimated effect toward zero (attenuation bias). Write the limit into your methods section, the part of a paper that explains how the data were built and analysed, in your own words.
To verify a variable is to compare it with an independent source that measured the same thing, ideally ground truth (values observed directly, such as a harvest weighed on the field). For a variable in your own research, name that source and the comparison a referee, the expert a journal asks to assess a submitted paper, would need to see.
Read outside economics. Questions come from noticing things, and you notice more when you read widely: history, geography, the other social sciences, good reporting, and the domain literature, meaning research from the field that studies your subject directly, such as hydrology for water use. Come with three things you read recently that were not economics, and what each one made you want to measure.
Where to take this next. How to learn a new method on your own. Start from a survey article and a replication package (the data and code a paper’s authors release so others can reproduce its results), then apply the method to data where you already know the answer before you trust it on new data.

title: 26 · Satellite I: on your machine
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 26 · Satellite I: on your machine
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Say what each sensor type records and which questions it can answer.
Match a sensor’s spatial, temporal and spectral resolution to a research question.
Compute NDVI from two bands and say what it proxies.
Choose between a ready-made product and classifying your own, and measure the accuracy of a map you classified.
Download one scene and process it in R on your own machine.

title: 26 · Satellite I: on your machine
text:
What we cover

Remote sensing (measuring the Earth’s surface from a distance, here from satellites) in economics:

Henderson, Storeygard & Weil (AER, 2012) measured economic growth from night lights seen from space.
Burchfield et al. (QJE, 2006) measured urban sprawl across the US from land use mapped on 30-metre cells.
Jack et al. (AER: Insights, 2025) detected crop-residue burning on farms in a randomized trial in Punjab, India, with a classifier trained on field-labelled pixels.

What each sensor records. A band is one range of light wavelengths, stored as its own grid of numbers.

Visible bands: a true-colour picture, close to what the eye sees.
Near-infrared, light just beyond red and invisible to the eye: healthy leaves reflect much of it.
Thermal infrared: heat given off by the surface, converted into surface temperature.
Radar: the sensor sends its own signal and records the echo, which shows surface roughness and moisture through cloud and at night.
Night lights: artificial light after dark, a stand-in for local economic activity.
Solar-induced fluorescence: the faint glow plants give off while using sunlight to grow, which tracks plant activity more closely than greenness does.

Three resolutions decide what a sensor can answer. Spatial resolution is the ground size of one pixel, such as 10 by 10 metres. Temporal resolution, or revisit time, is how often the satellite images the same place. Spectral resolution is how many bands it records and how narrow each one is. A sharper pixel usually comes with a longer wait between images, so confirm the pixel is small enough to resolve the unit you study, such as a field or a village.
Band algebra: NDVI (near-infrared minus red, divided by their sum, with values near 1 for dense green plants), and related indices for water and burned area. Read the index at a forest, a parking lot, a lake and an irrigated field, where you know roughly what to expect.
Land-cover products (ready-made maps labelling each pixel as forest, water, cropland, built-up land and so on), burned area and crop type, against supervised classification (training a model on pixels you labelled by hand so it labels all the others). NAIP’s 1-metre aerial imagery for the US helps with the labelling. Hold back part of your ground truth (labels collected on the ground or read from sharper imagery) to verify the map: measure its accuracy on those pixels, and compare your classes with a ready-made land-cover map over the same area.
One scene (one image of a fixed patch of ground on one date) end to end: find it, download it, read the bands with terra, apply the cloud mask (a layer marking pixels hidden by cloud or shadow), crop to your area and compute the index.
Big downloads: read the file listing, loop through download, extract and delete so the disk survives, cache the large intermediate with saveRDS(), and have the script beep when an hour-long job finishes.

title: 24 · Spatial II: rasters
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 24 · Spatial II: rasters
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Load, crop and align rasters with terra, and combine them with raster algebra.
Compute zonal statistics over polygons with exactextractr.
Choose between area and population weights, and predict which way the choice moves a county average.
Turn daily gridded weather into a county-by-day table.
Convert u/v wind components into speed and direction, and flag the areas downwind of a fire.

title: 24 · Spatial II: rasters
text:
What we cover

Published work built on rasters, grids of equal-size cells covering the ground, each holding one value such as temperature. Deschênes & Greenstone (AER, 2007) averaged 4-kilometre temperature and rainfall cells over each county’s farmland and related year-to-year swings in weather to farm profits, with degree days taken from weather stations. Dell, Jones & Olken (AEJ: Macro, 2012) averaged a global half-degree grid to countries, weighting cells by population or by land area, to estimate how hot years affect growth. Deryugina et al. (AER, 2019) used shifts in daily county wind direction, computed from gridded wind components, to estimate how fine particles affect elderly mortality and medical costs.
A raster is a matrix with coordinates attached. Resolution is the ground width of one cell; extent is the rectangle the grid covers. Raster algebra, arithmetic cell by cell across grids, needs matching resolution, extent, origin and map coordinate system, so first resample one grid onto the other’s cells or project it.
A zonal statistic summarises the cells inside each polygon, such as a county’s mean temperature; exactextractr weights each cell by its coverage fraction, the share inside the polygon. Area weights count a cell by its share of the county’s land, population weights by the people in it. The two differ most in large, thinly populated places.
Application: daily gridded weather to one row per county and day. Gridded weather products fill a grid with estimates from stations and satellites; a reanalysis rebuilds past weather by running old observations through a forecasting model. Hand-compute one county’s average and compare it with the table.
Application: the areas downwind of a fire, where the wind carries its smoke. Wind arrives as east-west (u) and north-south (v) components. Weather data reports where it comes from, clockwise from north; atan2(v, u) gives where it blows toward, counterclockwise from east. Convert first, then compare the flag with smoke imagery or monitor data.
The fast method: store the cell-to-county weights once as a sparse matrix (mostly zeros, so only the nonzero entries are kept), and each day’s county averages take one matrix multiply. Time it against the canned function with system.time() and verify the two agree.
Gridded products disagree. Several cover the same place with different answers, so name yours and the reason in the methods section.

title: 22 · Photographs II: classifying & counting
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 22 · Photographs II: classifying & counting
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Turn photos into image embeddings and train a simple classifier, a rule that assigns each photo to one of a few categories, on them.
Count cars and people in a photo with an object-detection model, and choose its confidence cutoff.
Pull street-level images, photos taken from roads by camera-carrying cars, for a set of locations and score them.
Score faces for emotion and state the ethics constraints that face data demands.
Measure each classifier’s agreement with hand labels on held-out photos, and the error of each count.

title: 22 · Photographs II: classifying & counting
text:
What we cover

What these methods have measured in economics. Adukia et al. (QJE, 2023) detected faces in a century of children’s-book illustrations and classified their skin colour, race, gender and age to measure who is shown and how that changed. Naik, Raskar & Hidalgo (AER P&P, 2016), a short proceedings paper, scored street-level images of 19 US cities for perceived safety and related the scores to density, income and inequality. Hu & Ma (JF, 2025) scored facial expressions, voice and words in startup pitch videos and found that positive delivery raises the odds of funding, with women judged more on delivery in single-gender teams.
Image embeddings: a model turns each photo into a long list of numbers, and photos that look alike get similar lists.
A simple classifier on the embeddings: a logistic regression with glm(), which turns the numbers into a probability between 0 and 1 that a label applies, explained step by step. It is trained on a few hundred photos with hand labels (the category a person assigned by looking), and some labelled photos are held out from training. The agreement rate, the share of held-out photos where the classifier matches the hand label, is the number you report.
Counting objects: object detection finds every car or person in a photo and marks each with a bounding box, the rectangle where it sits, and a confidence score between 0 and 1. Detections below the confidence cutoff are dropped, so the count you report depends on the cutoff you pick. Verify each count against a hand count on held-out photos, and look at the false positives (counting something that is not there) and false negatives (missing something that is).
Street-level imagery: what exists, its terms of use, and its coverage (which places and dates have imagery), which is uneven across both. Mapillary, a crowdsourced platform where people upload street photos from phones and dashcams, offers an open licence and a free API.
Faces and emotion: face detection finds where faces are, and a facial emotion classifier labels each face with an emotion such as happy or angry, scored against hand labels. Face recognition, matching a face to a named person, raises the sharpest privacy concerns. The ethics face data demands include consent, identifying people, and error rates that differ across groups, such as by skin tone or age.
Running the embedding and detection models yourself needs Python. A setup guide comes with the session materials, and their output is also provided.

title: 20 · Audio II: tone & emotion
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 20 · Audio II: tone & emotion
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Start from a transcript with word timestamps and speaker labels, and add measures of how each utterance (one unbroken turn by one speaker) was said.
Measure pauses and speaking rate from the word timestamps, and count filler words.
Extract pitch and energy for each utterance and compare each speaker with their own baseline.
Attach the scores of an emotion model to the utterance table.
Measure how closely a tone score agrees with a sample of utterances you rated by ear.

title: 20 · Audio II: tone & emotion
text:
What we cover

What vocal tone has measured in economics. Gorodnichenko, Pham & Talavera (AER, 2023) scored Federal Reserve chairs’ answers at press conferences with a voice-emotion model trained on actors’ labelled speech, and found that a positive tone raises share prices beyond what the words and the policy decision convey. Mayew & Venkatachalam (JF, 2012) measured managers’ positive and negative emotion from the audio of earnings calls, the quarterly calls where they present results, and found it predicts the firm’s future performance beyond the words used. Hu & Ma (JF, 2025) scored the delivery of startup pitch videos and found that positive delivery raises the odds of funding, while funded startups with the most positive pitches go on to underperform.
The starting point, loaded from file: one row per utterance with speaker, text, start and end, plus a timestamp for every word.
Timing measures: the pause before each answer (the silence between the question’s last word and the answer’s first), speaking rate in words per second, and filler words such as “um” and “uh”, sounds that fill a gap without adding meaning, counted with a pattern.
The waveform is the recorded sound stored as a long series of numbers, one per tiny slice of time; the sampling rate is how many per second, often 16,000 for speech. Pitch is how high or low a voice sounds, the number of vocal-cord vibrations per second, reported in hertz (Hz). Energy is the size of the wave’s swings, heard as loudness. Both are summarized per utterance and set against the speaker’s baseline, their own typical value.
Emotion models are trained on voice clips labelled by emotion and return a score for each label. They are least reliable on speech unlike their training data, so verify them on yours: draw a sample of utterances with a random seed so the draw repeats exactly, rate each by ear on a fixed scale before seeing the model’s score, then compare and listen to the clips where you disagree most.
Some of these models need Python and large installs. A setup guide comes with the session materials, and their output is also provided as files you read into R.
Text sentiment, a score for how positive or negative the words are regardless of delivery, set beside the vocal measures to find the utterances where the two disagree.
Application: the Federal Reserve chair’s tone of voice through the 2021-2023 inflation surge and around each rate decision, set beside the words.

title: 18 · Documents & scans
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 18 · Documents & scans
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Tell a born-digital PDF from a scanned one and pick the extraction method that fits.
Extract text and tables from a born-digital PDF.
Run OCR on a scanned page, and send a page image to a vision model.
Rebuild a table that runs across several pages.
Reconcile the rows you extracted with the totals printed on the page.
Recognize the two ways extraction fails: rows that go missing and numbers a model invents.

title: 18 · Documents & scans
text:
What we cover

Correia, Luck & Verner (QJE, 2026) ran OCR (software that reads the letters in a page image and writes them out as text) on national-bank balance sheets in the Comptroller of the Currency’s annual reports up to 1941, re-read the output by hand wherever assets did not equal liabilities plus capital, and added later records to build a bank panel from 1863 to 2024 showing that failures are predictable. Donaldson (AER, 2018) built district-level series of crop prices, output, rainfall and trade from colonial India’s printed government records, never digitized before, and showed that railroads cut trade costs and raised real incomes. Hanlon (REStat, 2024) digitized a century of weekly London death counts from the Registrar General’s printed reports, dated heavy fogs from the reports’ daily weather notes, and estimated the deaths that fog-trapped pollution caused. Archives still hold many tables nobody has turned into data.
Born-digital and scanned PDFs. A born-digital file is made by software and stores its words in a text layer you can select, search and copy. A scan is a picture of a page and holds no text until OCR runs; at a low resolution (dots per inch), OCR misreads more characters.
Table extraction (pulling a printed table’s rows and columns into a data frame) from born-digital files, OCR on scans, and a vision model, an AI model that takes a picture of a page and returns its text or table. Layout detection locates columns, rows, headings and footnotes before anything is read.
Multi-page tables that run across page breaks: headers that repeat, rows split across a break, and footnote markers (symbols attached to a value) mixed into the numbers.
In class: handwritten historical records, such as old restaurant menus with prices, census pages or ship logbooks, read by a vision model and compared with transcriptions volunteers typed by hand.
Choosing between OCR, a vision model and hand entry, by the number of pages and what an error would cost the analysis. Hand entry is usually double keyed: two people type the same table, and every cell where they differ is re-read against the page.
The two common failures. Partial extraction drops rows without warning, and fabrication returns a plausible number that is not on the page. Reconcile the extracted rows with the total row most statistical tables print, and verify that a balance sheet obeys its accounting identity (a relation that must hold exactly, such as assets equal to liabilities plus capital). A sum that falls short points to dropped rows, and a cell that breaks the identity points to a misread or invented number.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Write regular expressions with stringr, from literal matches to groups.
Extract structured fields, such as dates and dollar amounts, from messy text.
Count word frequencies in a set of documents after dropping stop words.
Score each document with a sentiment dictionary by counting its positive and negative words.
Pair every pattern with a should-match test and a should-not-match test.

title: 16 · Text I: regex
text:
What we cover

Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016) built a keyword index, the monthly share of newspaper articles with a term from each of three lists (economy, policy, uncertainty), and had people read 12,000 articles to confirm it tracks policy uncertainty. Shapiro & Wilson (REStud, 2022) scored the tone of Fed meeting transcripts with a finance word list, compared the scores with research assistants’ ratings of a sample, and estimated the Fed’s implicit inflation target at about 1.5 percent. Djourelova (AER, 2023) counted articles with the phrase “illegal immigrant” before and after the Associated Press banned it, and found that exposed readers grew less supportive of restrictive immigration policy.
stringr and regular expressions (regex), written patterns that describe the text to find: literals, character classes (a set in brackets, any one of which can match, such as [0-9]), quantifiers (how often the piece before may repeat, such as + for one or more), anchors (^ and $ pin the start and the end) and groups.
Extracting fields with capture groups, the parts of a pattern inside parentheses that come out as their own column. Each pattern carries should-match and should-not-match tests, strings it must catch and strings it must skip, rerun after every change. A row caught by mistake is a false positive; one missed is a false negative.
The corpus: the Federal Reserve’s policy statements and press-conference transcripts, provided as a file.
Counting words: split each document in the corpus (the full set of documents you analyze) into tokens, usually single words, tabulate with table(), drop stop words such as “the” and “of”, and compare term frequencies (a word’s share of the document’s words).
Dictionary sentiment: a published list of positive and negative words, a count of each per document, and a net tone score (positive minus negative, over the word count). A dictionary built for one domain misreads another; “liability” and “tax” carry no sentiment in a company report. A human audit reads the top- and bottom-scoring documents and a random sample by hand to verify the score matches a person’s judgment.
Readability metrics in one slide, and a one-line fix for a broken character encoding, the rule that stores letters as numbers (“café” read with the wrong rule shows up as “cafÃ©”).
Regex and word counts are cheap and give the same answer on every run, which makes them the first thing to try on a new corpus.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
text: Materials for this session are not published yet. They appear here before class.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Request data from an API and turn the JSON response into a data frame.
Store an API key in ~/.Renviron and read it from R.
Page through results within the rate limit, and compare the rows you received with the total the API reports.
Save each raw response so the pipeline reruns from disk.
Send a prompt to a large language model through its provider’s API from R, read the reply, and count the tokens it used.
Convert UTC timestamps to local time.

title: 14 · Channels I: APIs
text:
What we cover

Published work built on an API, a service that lets your program request data from another computer and receive a structured reply. Akbar et al. (AER, 2023) queried Google Maps for 57 million simulated car trips in 180 Indian cities, choosing destinations through the Google Places API, to measure travel speed and congestion, then compared them with data on actual trips. Fujiwara, Müller & Schwarz (JEEA, 2024) pulled the profiles of about 658,000 followers of a festival’s Twitter account through Twitter’s API, and used their join dates and locations to estimate Twitter’s effect on US presidential votes. From finance, Lopez-Lira & Tang (JFE, 2026) sent firm news headlines to a large language model (a program trained on vast amounts of text that writes a reply to what you send) through its provider’s API, scored each as good or bad news, and tested whether the scores predict stock returns.
Every call has the same shape: a key, a request and a response. The response carries a status code (200 means it worked, 429 too many requests) and, when it worked, data in JSON, a plain-text format of named values and nested lists that you turn into a data frame.
Endpoints (the web address that answers one kind of request) and query parameters (named values, such as a year or a state, that narrow what comes back). Long results arrive in pages you request one after another (pagination), within a rate limit, the most requests a service accepts from you per minute, hour or day. Compare the number of rows you collected with the total the API reports.
An API key is a private string that identifies you and counts your requests. Keys live in ~/.Renviron as environment variables (named values set outside your code and loaded when R starts) and are read with Sys.getenv(), so they never appear in a script or a commit.
Saving the raw response, the reply exactly as the server sent it, with saveRDS() and reading it back with readRDS(), so the pipeline still runs when the server changes or goes down.
A model call sends a prompt (the instructions and material in one request) from R to a large language model, with its key stored the same way. Read the raw reply to verify anything parsed from it. The same request sent twice can come back worded differently, and many current models do not let you turn that variation off, so the saved reply is the record. Each reply reports its usage in tokens, the chunks of text a model reads, writes and bills by.
Timestamps that arrive in UTC, the world reference clock, converted to local time with lubridate, daylight saving included.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
Slides · Source
How to draw a figure to a journal’s rules: first by asking an agent to match a picture of the finished figure, then by writing each journal’s rules in a file that the R code, a checking script and an agent all read. One figure runs through the session: county maps of how much farmland values and home values rose from 1940 to 2022, drawn for Nature and for the American Economic Review. The project is a zip file. Its data, including two licensed files, are a separate download for the class, with a Cornell NetID:
https://cornell.box.com/s/mx2eg35oytjt2a7xjsapuh8tbq2e6edc
Replace the project’s data folder with the data folder in that zip.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
Figure 1, ready for Nature


Question: did farmland values rise more in counties where home values rose more?
a Farmland value per acre (Census of Agriculture) and b median value of an owner-occupied home (1940 census; 2018–2022 American Community Survey), each as its 2022 value divided by its 1940 value. c One against the other, 2,985 counties.
Real terms: each year’s dollars divided by the consumer price index. 183 mm wide, Nature’s two-column width.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
Figure 1 with R’s default settings




The same data, with pdf(), par(mfrow = c(1, 3)), map(fill = TRUE), cut(x, 6) and plot(), with nothing else set. The code is at the start of Part 2.

A 7 × 7 in page; no journal prints that size, and two thirds of it is blank
Fonts not embedded: the file holds no copy of the typeface
Six classes of equal width: one outlier stretches them, and 3,052 of 3,053 counties get the same red
No key, and black county borders that turn the East solid
The x label is a variable name, d$house_ratio; the y label does not show

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
Two kinds of requirements


Technical specifications, set by the journal and measured in the file:

Width and height of the file
Text size and line weight, in points (1 pt = 1/72 inch)
Fonts embedded: a copy of each typeface inside the file
A vector file (PDF or EPS, sharp at any zoom), no pictures inside

Readability, judged by looking at the figure:

Can a reader see the main comparison?
Is any text cut off, overlapping, or on top of data?
Do titles and labels say what is shown, with units?
Can every class be told apart, in gray and by a colour-blind reader?
Do the class breaks spread the data across the classes?



A vector file stores shapes and text as geometry, as PDF and EPS do, so it stays sharp at any zoom; a PNG is a grid of pixels. An embedded font is a copy of the typeface inside the file, so the figure prints the same on any computer. A point (pt) is 1/72 inch.
The technical specifications can be checked by a program that reads the PDF: each answer is a number, and the journal gives the range it accepts. Readability needs someone to look at the figure: a person, or an agent that looks at an image of it. The project splits the work along the same line: a script measures the specifications, and an agent judges readability (see “Agents that review and redraw a figure” below).

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Nature and AER requirements for size, fonts and text
text:
Nature and AER requirements for size, fonts and text








Requirement
Nature’s words
The AER’s words




Width
“Nature’s standard figure sizes are 89 mm wide (single column) and 183 mm wide (double column).”
Not stated


Font
“Lettering should be in a sans-serif typeface, preferably Helvetica or Arial, the same font throughout all figures in the paper.”
Not stated


Text size
“Maximum text size for all other text should be 7 pt; minimum text size should be 5 pt.”
Not stated


Panel labels
“Separate panels in multi-part figures should each be labelled with 8 pt bold, upright (not italic) a, b, c.”
For file names: “use letters for indicating individual panels (e.g., Figure1a.ppt, Figure1b.ppt, Figure1c.ppt, etc.)”


Line weight
“Line weights and strokes should be set between 0.25 and 1 pt at the final size”
Not stated



Pages: Nature, final submission and preparing figures; AER style guide. Not stated: the rule is yours to set, once for the whole paper.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Nature and AER requirements for files, colour and labels
text:
Nature and AER requirements for files, colour and labels








Requirement
Nature’s words
The AER’s words




File format
“Vector EPS or PDF format for figures containing line drawings and graphs”; “Embed fonts (True Type 2 or 42)”
“Figures must be supplied as vector-based graphics in one of the following formats—vector PDF, EPS, AI, WMF, or PPT.”


Photographs and images
“All photographic images must be supplied at a minimum of 300 dpi at the maximum size they can be used.”
“Photographs and other images (maps, screenshots, etc.) should be provided at 300 dpi”


Colour
“Colour artwork can be provided in RGB (recommended) or CMYK format.”; “An accessible colour palette to be used”
Not stated


Labels
“All axes to be labelled with units in parentheses, e.g. Data (unit)”
“If there are variables (italics) or matrices and vectors (boldface) in figures, they should be designated as such.”



Pages: Nature, final submission and preparing figures; AER style guide. The AER also asks that the files “correspond to the figures in your accompanying PDF”.
The quotes are copied from the journals’ pages; the project’s specs/nature.yml and specs/aer.yml hold the same sentences, each with the page it comes from. One Nature sentence keeps a typo: “Do not rasterize or covert text to outlines.” The AER’s figures section also says “Source notes, if any, should be placed after other notes related to the figure.”

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: When journals ask for the final figure files
text:
When journals ask for the final figure files

Nature: “The Nature journals are flexible with regard to the format of initial submissions.” “If revisions are requested, the editor will provide detailed formatting instructions at that time.”
AER: “Adherence to the journal’s Style Guide is required for accepted articles but is optional at the time of submission.”
PNAS: each figure as a separate high-quality PDF or EPS file, with the revised manuscript.
Journals ask for the final files at revision (Nature, PNAS) or at acceptance (AER). With the journal’s rules in a file and a figure script that reads them (Part 3), the final files are one run of the script.

Pages: Nature, initial submission; AER, submissions; PNAS, how to submit a manuscript.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: What studies show about presentation and referees
text:
What studies show about presentation and referees


An experiment on writing: Feld, Lines and Ross (JEBO, 2024)

Professional editors improved the English of 30 economics papers, with the layout unchanged.
Economists rated the edited versions 0.2 SD higher and were 8.4 percentage points more likely to accept them for a conference.

Referees’ reasons for rejecting: Bordage (Acad Med, 2001)

On 123 conference submissions that at least one reviewer wanted to reject, text difficult to follow and defective tables or figures were among the ten most common reasons.

A format rule and authors: Card and DellaVigna (JEP, 2014)

After the AER capped submissions at 40 pages in 2008, 21% came in at 39 or 40 pages, up from 6%.

The look of the page: Huang (arXiv, 2018)

A model that saw only page images of computer-vision papers flagged half of the workshop papers (a stand-in for rejected ones) and 0.4% of the conference papers. Referees were not part of the test.



Takeaway: clear writing and readable figures help a paper with referees. No study has sent the same paper to referees in the journal’s format and in a plain one.
Feld, Lines and Ross had 30 economists rate papers written by economics PhD students, each economist seeing either the original or the language-edited version of a paper, never both; most edits were to the title, abstract and introduction, and the gains came from the papers that were poorly written to begin with. Bordage analysed the written comments of reviewers on 151 manuscripts submitted to a medical education conference; excellent writing was among the main strengths of the papers accepted unanimously. Card and DellaVigna studied the AER’s page limit; authors met it partly by tightening spacing and margins. Huang’s “weak” papers were workshop papers standing in for rejections, so the result shows that page layout carries information about a paper; it does not test how referees respond to layout. A wider review of this literature, with about fifty studies, found no test of whether following a journal’s format at first submission changes referees’ decisions.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
Matching Nature’s requirements in R
Draw the file at the size it will print. Then every size you set is the size the reader sees.







Nature requires
Setting in R




89 mm wide, one column (183 mm for two)
cairo_pdf(width = 89 / 25.4): R takes inches


Helvetica or Arial, embedded in the file
family = "Helvetica"; cairo_pdf() embeds the font


Text from 5 to 7 pt
pointsize = 7 for 7-pt text; cex.axis = 6 / 7 for 6-pt tick labels (printed size = pointsize × cex)


Panel letters, 8 pt bold
mtext("a", font = 2, cex = 8 / 7)


Lines from 0.25 to 1 pt
lwd = 0.5 / 0.75 for a 0.5-pt line (lwd = 1 is 0.75 pt)


A vector file
cairo_pdf() writes one



Point (pt): a length, 1/72 inch or about 0.35 mm; a font’s size in points is the height from the top of an h to the bottom of a p. With layout() or mfrow and three or more rows or columns, R multiplies every text size by 0.66 (0.83 for two by two): add par(cex = 1) after it.
A journal places a figure at its column width and scales everything in it by the same factor, so sizes only mean something at the printed width. Open the file at that width, in inches (25.4 mm to the inch), and set the text size you want printed. cairo_pdf() writes a vector PDF with the fonts embedded; base R’s pdf() names the font without embedding it. Both write a page 7 × 7 inches unless you give width and height. The Plots pane in RStudio has no fixed size: a figure saved from it with Export takes the pane’s current size, or what you type in the dialog, so the same code gives different files on different screens.

     xlab = "Speed (mph)",

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
Setting text sizes in R







You set
Printed size




pointsize = 7 when you open the device
7 pt for text at cex = 1


cex.axis = 6/7
tick labels at 6 pt


mtext("a", cex = 8/7, font = 2)
an 8-pt bold panel letter


layout() or mfrow with 3 or more panels
every size × 0.66, until par(cex = 1)



Text size in points = pointsize × cex. pointsize is the size of ordinary text, in points (1/72 inch), for the whole file.
cex is a multiplier, not a size. The base it multiplies is the pointsize the device was opened with, 12 unless you say otherwise. layout() and par(mfrow = ) quietly set cex to 0.66 when there are three or more rows or columns (0.83 for exactly two by two), so a three panel figure drawn at pointsize 7 prints its text at 4.6 pt unless par(cex = 1) comes right after layout().

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
Setting line widths in R

On R’s PDF devices, “Line widths are multiples of 1/96 inch”: lwd = 1 is 0.75 pt.
Measured in a cairo_pdf() file before class: lwd 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 drew lines of 0.375, 0.75, 1.5 and 3 pt.
Nature’s 0.25 to 1 pt is lwd 0.33 to 1.33.



R Console: writes lines.pdf, three lines at 0.25, 0.5 and 1 pt

pt_to_lwd <- function(pt) pt / 0.75     # also in the project's R/fig_style.R
cairo_pdf("lines.pdf", width = 89 / 25.4, height = 30 / 25.4)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0.5, 3.5), axes = FALSE, ann = FALSE)
abline(h = 1:3, lwd = pt_to_lwd(c(0.25, 0.5, 1)))
dev.off()

Source: R’s help page, ?pdf. The measurement converted the PDF to SVG with pdftocairo and read each stroke’s width.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Categorical, sequential and diverging colour scales
text:
Categorical, sequential and diverging colour scales






Deuteranopia: red–green colour blindness. The eye lacks the cones that sense green, so reds and greens look alike.

“About 1 in 12 men have color vision deficiency”, most often red and green (National Eye Institute). Okabe-Ito colours: Wong (Nature Methods, 2011), the paper Nature’s guide cites. Simulation: Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (IEEE TVCG, 2009), full severity.
In the image, Use and Avoid are for readers with colour blindness. A tick means the colours stay apart (categorical) or keep their order (sequential, diverging) in that column; a cross means they do not. Only the sequential scales also pass in grayscale, so a figure with categories or a diverging scale that may be printed in gray needs labels, shapes or line types as well as colour.
Pick the kind of scale from the data. Categorical colours mark groups with no order, such as regions; they only need to look different from one another, and the Okabe-Ito colours in palette.colors() stay different for readers with deuteranopia. Sequential colours show values that rise in one direction; the lightness must rise with them, from light to dark, so the order survives in gray and for colour-blind readers. rainbow() fails that test: its yellow and green are lighter than its red and blue, so the middle classes look brighter than the ends. Diverging colours show values above and below a midpoint that means something, such as zero change; two hues meet at a light middle. Red and green at the two ends is the classic failure, since a reader with deuteranopia sees both ends as olive.
Figure 1’s blue-to-red scale runs through green, yellow and orange, a rainbow scale: easy to tell apart in colour, and the checks show its cost, with green and orange alike for deuteranopia and close in gray.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
The data









Farmland value per acre
Median home value




1940
Census of Agriculture, county file by Haines, Fishback and Rhode (ICPSR)
1940 census, via IPUMS NHGIS


2022
Census of Agriculture, NASS Quick Stats
American Community Survey, 2018–2022, via IPUMS NHGIS


Counties
3,053
3,016




Real terms: prices rose 20.9-fold from 1940 to 2022 (consumer price index, BLS). 2,985 counties have both.
The median county’s farmland was worth 7.3 times its 1940 value in 2022, its homes 5.5 times. Home values are not adjusted for quality: a 2022 home is larger and better equipped.

ICPSR and IPUMS NHGIS: archives that distribute research data under terms that forbid passing the files on; each user needs a free account. Median: the value with half the homes above and half below.
Farmland value is the Census of Agriculture’s value of land and buildings per acre. The 1940 values come from Haines, Fishback and Rhode’s county files (ICPSR 35206), part 1; that file gives three Kansas and Georgia counties a neighbour’s code, which 2_clean_data.R corrects. The 2022 values come from NASS’s Quick Stats API, which goes back only to the 1997 census at the county level. The 1940 median home value is NHGIS table NT74 from the 1940 census, the first census of housing; the 2022 value is the American Community Survey median for 2018–2022, in 2022 dollars (NHGIS). Both are deflated with the consumer price index for all urban consumers. The 1940 period comes before the Interstate highways, which began in 1956.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
The default code for Figure 1




code/figure1_default.R (part); needs data_clean/ from code/2_clean_data.R

library(maps)
d <- readRDS("data_clean/counties.rds")
poly <- map("county", plot = FALSE, namesonly = TRUE)
fips <- sprintf("%05d",
  county.fips$fips[match(poly, county.fips$polyname)])
pdf("figures/default/figure1.pdf")
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
map("county", fill = TRUE,
    col = heat.colors(6)[cut(d$land_ratio[match(fips, d$fips)], 6)])
title("Farmland")
map("county", fill = TRUE,
    col = heat.colors(6)[cut(d$house_ratio[match(fips, d$fips)], 6)])
title("Houses")
plot(d$house_ratio, d$land_ratio)
dev.off()






d has one row per county. land_ratio and house_ratio are the 2022 value divided by the 1940 value.
Download the project (a zip file), then its data (Cornell NetID login): replace the project’s data folder with the one in the data zip.

cut(x, 6) splits the range from the smallest to the largest value into six equal parts. One county’s farmland is worth 924 times its 1940 value, so the first class runs from 0.4 to about 154 and holds every county but one.

What matching a picture costs

Every number is typed into the script: the page size, the text sizes, the colours, and positions measured in the picture’s pixels.
Some numbers are guesses: the titles came out up to 0.35 pt over Nature’s limit, the panel letters 0.65 pt short.
The same prompt gives different numbers on each run.
The next figure in the paper needs the same work again.
A second journal needs a new target picture and another run.
Nothing in the script says where a number came from.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Why write the requirements in a file
text:
Why write the requirements in a file

In Part 2 the agent had only a picture, so it guessed the sizes. With the rules in a file, it reads them.
The file is specs/nature.yml, a short text file of Nature’s requirements: widths, fonts, text sizes, panel labels, line weights.
Each requirement carries the journal’s own words and the page they come from. We call the file the spec, short for specification.
Three programs read it:

R, to set the size and fonts when it draws
The checking script, tools/check_fig.R, to measure the PDF
Claude Code, when it writes or edits figure code

Edit a value in the file, and every figure drawn after that uses the new value.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
What a YAML file is


What it is: a plain-text file of settings, one name: value per line, ending in .yml or .yaml.

Indenting by two spaces puts a value inside the name above it.
{min: 5, max: 7} is the one-line form of min: 5 and max: 7 indented under the name.
A # after a space starts a comment.
Text with a colon followed by a space goes in quotes.

What uses it: settings that a person writes and a program reads.

The header at the top of a Quarto document, and _quarto.yml
GitHub’s automated jobs (.github/workflows/)

What reads it: Quarto and GitHub, for their own settings · R, with the yaml package · Python, with PyYAML · an agent, as text




R Console; needs the yaml package (install.packages("yaml"))

library(yaml)
s <- read_yaml(text = "
text_pt:
  value: {min: 5, max: 7}
")
s$text_pt$value$max      # a list inside a list
#> [1] 7

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
The spec file for Nature


specs/nature.yml (part)

text_pt:
  value: {min: 5, max: 7}
  quote: "Maximum text size for all other text should be 7 pt; minimum text size should be 5 pt."
  source: final

panel_label:
  value: {pt: 8, bold: true, case: lower, placement: inside}
  quote: "Separate panels in multi-part figures should each be labelled with 8 pt bold, upright (not italic) a, b, c."
  source: final (size, bold, lower case); house (letter at top left)

line_pt:
  value: {min: 0.25, max: 1}
  quote: "Line weights and strokes should be set between 0.25 and 1 pt at the
    final size (lines thinner than 0.25 pt may vanish in print)."
  source: final



Each rule has three parts:

value: what R and the checking script use
quote: Nature’s sentence, word for word
source: the page, listed under pages: at the top of the file, or house for our own choice where the pages say nothing

This file comes with the project, with each quote checked against Nature’s pages.
Later in this part, live, Claude Code writes it again from Nature’s pages.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: A script that checks a PDF against the spec file
text:
A script that checks a PDF against the spec file


With Nature’s rules in a file, a script can measure any PDF against them.
tools/check_fig.R reads specs/<journal>.yml, measures the PDF, and prints one line per rule: PASS or FAIL, and what it measured.
It works on any PDF figure, drawn in R, Python or anything else, for any journal with a spec file.
It checks the rules the spec sets as numbers:

Width and height, fonts and whether they are embedded
Text sizes and panel letters
Line weights, and pictures pasted inside the PDF

Readability is left to a person, or to an agent that looks at the figure.
It comes in the project zip, in tools/, written with Claude Code before class: 137 lines of R.
It needs poppler, a free set of command-line tools that read PDFs (on a Mac, brew install poppler), and the R packages yaml and magick.

title: 12 · Publication graphics

text:
Asking Claude Code for a checking script

each with the journal's words. Write tools/check_fig.R, an R script run as
  Rscript tools/check_fig.R <pdf> <journal>
that measures the PDF against specs/<journal>.yml and prints one line per
rule, PASS or FAIL, with what it measured: the page width and height
(pdfinfo), the fonts and whether each is embedded (pdffonts), the size of
every word of text (pdftotext -bbox), the panel letters, and the line
weights (pdftocairo -svg). Read every number from the spec file; type none
into the script. Test it on the PDFs in pdfs/. pdfs/cars-nature.pdf was
drawn 89 x 70 mm with 7-pt text, 6-pt tick labels, an 8-pt bold letter a
and 0.5-pt lines, with embedded fonts, so it should pass every Nature rule.

On Claude Code’s Part 2 figure it found the same two failures as the project’s script. It passed the target.
On the default figure, which has no panel letters, it printed PASS for the letters (“single panel?”). The project’s script prints FAIL.
Takeaway: test a checker an agent wrote on PDFs whose right answers you know.

text:
How the checking script measures the width


Terminal, in the project folder: the tool the script runs for the width

pdfinfo figures/default/figure1.pdf

Page size:       504 x 504 pts



504 pt × 25.4 / 72 = 177.8 mm. The spec allows 89, 120 or 183 mm (one column, a column and a half, two columns), so the width fails.
The other checks follow the same steps, with other tools that read the PDF:

pdffonts: each font, and whether it is embedded
pdftotext -bbox: a box around every word; its height is the text size
pdftocairo -svg: every line, with its width in points

The script runs these tools and compares each result with Nature’s number.


Text sizes are exact for embedded fonts and read about half a point low for fonts that are not embedded.

The second run marked the rules the pages do not state as house rules: where the panel letter goes, and colours that stay distinct in gray.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: The spec file for the AER
text:
The spec file for the AER


specs/aer.yml (part)

panel_label:
  value: {placement: title}
  quote: "Be sure to label your figure files clearly, taking special care to use
    letters for indicating individual panels (e.g., Figure1a.ppt, Figure1b.ppt,
    Figure1c.ppt, etc.)."
  source: style (letters in file names); house ("Panel A." in the title)

width_mm:
  value: {panel: 115}
  quote: not stated
  source: house

text_pt:
  value: {min: 7, max: 9}
  quote: not stated
  source: house

House rule: one the journal does not set, chosen once for the whole paper and marked source: house. The AER’s style guide sets the file format, letters in the names of panel files, and where source notes go. Our house rules: one file per panel, “Panel A.” in the title, panels 115 mm wide, text 7 to 9 pt, lines 0.5 to 1.5 pt, colours that stay distinct in gray.

Live demo: Claude Code rewrites the script to read the spec files


Prompt to paste into Claude Code, in match/, after copying the project's specs/ into it

code/figure1_default.R draws Figure 1 for Nature, with every width, font,
text size and line weight typed into the script. specs/nature.yml and
specs/aer.yml hold each journal's rules, with the journal's words.

3. Run it for both journals and check the PDFs with pdfinfo and pdffonts.
Do not print the data; you do not need to look at it. When you finish,
list what you changed.


The goal: take the typed numbers out of Claude Code’s Part 2 script, so that one word at the top picks the journal.
Claude Code runs live, in match/, after cp -R ../specs . copies in the spec files. It takes about four minutes.

text:
What the rewrite produced

R/fig_style.R, 92 lines: read_spec(), open_fig(), a panel-label function, and one it added unasked, to undo the text shrink of R’s layout().
code/figure1.R, 128 lines, with no width, font, text size or line weight typed in.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: open_fig() opens the PDF with the spec’s settings
text:
open_fig() opens the PDF with the spec’s settings


R/fig_style.R (part); runs in R from the project folder; needs the yaml package

read_spec <- function(journal) {
  r <- read_yaml(file.path("specs", paste0(journal, ".yml")))
  list(journal  = journal,
       width_mm = r$width_mm$value,
       font     = r$font$value,
       text_pt  = r$text_pt$value,
       label    = r$panel_label$value,
       line_pt  = r$line_pt$value,
       panels   = r$file$value$panels)
}

open_fig <- function(path, spec, width, height_mm) {
  cairo_pdf(path, width = spec$width_mm[[width]] / 25.4,
            height = height_mm / 25.4,
            pointsize = spec$text_pt$max, family = spec$font)
  par(las = 1, mgp = c(1.5, 0.4, 0), tcl = -0.3, lwd = line_lwd(spec))
}


open_fig() is a wrapper: a short function that calls other functions with some arguments filled in.
It passes the spec’s width, font, text size and line weight to cairo_pdf() and par(). Figure scripts never type them.
Try it in R from the project folder, no data needed: source("R/fig_style.R"), open_fig("cars.pdf", read_spec("nature"), "single", 70) ("single" is a width named in the spec), plot(cars), dev.off().

title: 12 · Publication graphics
12 · Publication graphics
text:
Drawing the two maps


code/3_figure1.R (part); runs once data/ holds the two licensed files

draw_county_map <- function(ratio, letter) {
  poly <- map("county", plot = FALSE, namesonly = TRUE)
  fips <- sprintf("%05d", county.fips$fips[match(poly, county.fips$polyname)])
  cls  <- findInterval(ratio[match(fips, d$fips)], misc$breaks) + 1
  fill <- col$classes[cls]
  fill[is.na(fill)] <- col$no_data
  map("county", projection = "albers", parameters = c(29.5, 45.5),
      fill = TRUE, col = fill, border = fill,
      lwd = pt_to_lwd(spec$line_pt$min), mar = par("mar"))
  map("state", add = TRUE, ...,  boundary = FALSE, col = "white",
      lwd = line_lwd(spec))
  draw_panel_title(letter, title[[letter]], spec)
}


county.fips matches each map polygon to its county code. Breaks at 2, 4, 8 and 16: each class doubles.

The map polygons are named “state,county” ("iowa,story"); the county.fips table that comes with the maps package turns each name into the five-digit county code the data use. findInterval() puts each county in a class. Drawing each county’s border in its own fill colour hides the hairline gaps a PDF viewer shows between polygons. The state lines are drawn on top with boundary = FALSE, which leaves out the coastline, and with the same projection centre as the first call (the ... stands for orientation = .Last.projection()$orientation; without it the states are drawn off-centre).

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
Drawing the scatter plot


code/3_figure1.R (part); runs once data/ holds the two licensed files

x <- log(both$house_ratio)
y <- log(both$land_ratio)
lim <- log(c(1, 64))
out <- x < lim[1] | x > lim[2] | y < lim[1] | y > lim[2]
xc  <- pmin(pmax(x, lim[1]), lim[2])          # outside the range: at the edge
yc  <- pmin(pmax(y, lim[1]), lim[2])
plot(xc[!out], yc[!out], pch = 16, cex = 0.3, col = col$points,
     axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", xlim = lim, ylim = lim)
points(xc[out], yc[out], pch = 2, cex = 0.5)   # open triangles
cuts <- sort(x)[round(seq(1, length(x), length.out = 21))]
bin  <- findInterval(x, cuts, rightmost.closed = TRUE, all.inside = TRUE)
points(tapply(x, bin, mean), tapply(yc, bin, mean), pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
tk <- c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64)
axis(1, at = log(tk), labels = tk, cex.axis = cex_small(spec))


Log axes: each tick doubles. The black dots are the means in 20 bins of about 149 counties each, sorted by home value.
13 counties fall outside 1 to 64; they are drawn as triangles on the edge and counted in the key.

A log scale puts a doubling at the same distance anywhere on the axis, which is what a multiple needs: 2 to 4 is as far as 16 to 32. The bins have equal counts, found by sorting the home values and cutting them at every twentieth of the list. findInterval() assigns each county to its bin and tapply() takes the mean in each. Points outside the axes are the ones a reader is most likely to misread, so they get their own symbol and a count in the key.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Setting up an agent in Claude Code
text:
Setting up an agent in Claude Code


.claude/agents/figure-critic.md (top)

---
name: figure-critic
description: Checks a figure PDF against a journal spec in specs/ and
  reports what to change, most serious first. Use after a figure is drawn
  or changed. It reports only; it never edits files.
tools: Bash, Read, Glob, Grep
---


Claude Code reads the description to decide when to use the agent, and gives it only the tools listed: no Edit, no Write.
Subagent: a second Claude session with its own instructions, started by the first for one task. Context: everything a session has read so far. The critic starts with none of the builder’s.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
The critic agent’s instructions



.claude/agents/figure-critic.md (body, shortened)

1. Measure. Run `Rscript tools/check_fig.R <pdf> <journal>`. Use these
   numbers. Never estimate a size, a width or a line weight from a picture.

2. Look. Open check/<file>/print.png (the figure at its printed size),
   gray.png and deutan.png. Judge what code cannot measure:
   - Can a reader see the figure's main comparison without help?
   - Is any text clipped, overlapping, or covering data?
   - Do titles and axis labels say what is shown, with units?
   - Does the legend match what is drawn? Can every class be told apart?
   - Are class breaks chosen so the data spread across the classes?

3. Trace. Read the script and find the line behind each finding.

Report a numbered list, most serious first: what is wrong; the rule it
breaks, quoting the spec, or "judgment"; what was measured or seen; the
line of code to change. Do not edit any file.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
What the critic looks at


The checking script also writes the figure at its printed size, as a reader with deuteranopia sees it, and in gray.
The agent judges what has no number: whether the comparison reads, labels and units, classes that merge, breaks that bunch the data.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: The critic’s report from a test run
text:
The critic’s report from a test run

The maps show no data. cut(x, 6) makes six equal classes; one outlier stretches them, and 3,052 counties land in the lowest. Lines 14 and 17.
No key, so the colours mean nothing.
County borders at 0.75 pt turn the East solid black.
Two outliers rule the scatter. Use log axes and small filled points.
Colours (spec: accessible): heat.colors(6) loses its order in gray and for colour-blind readers.
Width 177.8 mm; Nature allows 89, 120 or 183 mm.
Fonts not embedded, 0 of 2. Use cairo_pdf().
Text 7.4 to 9.2 pt, above 7 pt. Set pointsize = 7.
No panel letters.
Axis labels are variable names, with no units; the y label does not appear at all.

Shortened from a test run: 86 seconds; Claude Code, the prompt on the previous slide, October 2026. It passed height, font family, line weight and vector content, and edited nothing.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Exercise: accept or reject a critic’s findings
text:
Exercise: accept or reject a critic’s findings

ExerciseSolution


A critic’s report on figures/default/figure1.pdf, checked against specs/nature.yml. Four minutes, no code. Mark each finding accept, reject or needs a check, with the reason. The checking script’s output is on “The checking script on three versions of Figure 1”.

Width is 177.8 mm; Nature allows 89, 120 or 183 mm.
Fonts are not embedded: 0 of 2.
Six equal-width classes put 3,052 of 3,053 counties in one class.
The panel titles are about 6 pt, so they meet Nature’s 5 to 7 pt.
The axis labels are variable names, with no units.
Use a serif font such as Times for the axis labels, to match the paper’s text.

Two answers to compare with the room: which findings you reject, and why.



Reject 4. The checking script measured the titles at 9.2 pt, above Nature’s 7 pt. “About 6 pt” is a guess from the picture, and it is wrong in the direction that hides a failure.
Reject 6. Nature asks for “a sans-serif typeface, preferably Helvetica or Arial”. The finding is a taste that contradicts the spec.
Accept 1, 2, 3 and 5. Each matches a measurement or what the figure shows.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: The critic’s second report, after the fixes
text:
The critic’s second report, after the fixes

Accepted, from the critic’s report on the spec-built figure: a palette with even steps in lightness (replaced later; see “Decisions you make as the author”); white for no data; triangles for counties outside the axes; both axes from 1 to 64; “real” and “log scale” in the labels. Declined: finer class breaks.
The builder made the five changes in code/3_figure1.R, drew both journals, checked each file, and listed three layout changes it made unasked (two-line axis labels, wider margins, a raised key).
The second report: no rule broken. It asked again for other class breaks, and found a legend symbol too faint to see, a title not aligned with the others, and means taken from the values moved to the edge.

Test runs before class, October 2026: the builder took 317 seconds, the second critic run 75 seconds. The figure on “Figure 1, ready for Nature” is the builder’s.
The last finding is a small error in the code the builder kept: the binned means use yc, the values moved to the edge of the axis, where they should use y, the values themselves. Thirteen of 2,985 counties are affected, and the dots barely move. The critic found it because its instructions send it to the code as well as to the pictures. The finding about class breaks came back a second time: the critic does not know that the author already decided, and it should not stop asking.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: The builder agent, which edits the code
text:
The builder agent, which edits the code


.claude/agents/figure-builder.md (body, shortened)

- Draw every figure through R/fig_style.R. Never set a width, height,
  font, point size, line weight or panel letter by hand; those come
  from specs/<journal>.yml.
- Change only figure code. Never change data/, data_clean/ or the
  scripts that build them. Ask before adding a package.
- Apply only the findings you were given. If a finding looks wrong,
  say so instead of applying it.
- After a change, draw the figure for each journal, run
  tools/check_fig.R on each file, and report the FAIL lines and the diff.


The builder can edit files; the critic cannot. Each starts fresh, so the critic judges the figure without the builder’s reasons for it.
You pass findings from one to the other, after reading them.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Decisions you make as the author
text:
Decisions you make as the author

The question. Did farmland values rise more where home values rose more, from 1940 (before the Interstate highways) to 2022?
What the reader compares. Two maps with one key, and the scatter beside them.
The class breaks. Classes that each double, because “twice as much” is easy to read.
The colours. Five hues from blue to red make each class easy to find on the map. The cost: green and orange look alike for deuteranopia and in gray.
Which changes to keep, after reading each one against the measurement and the spec.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
What to take away

Open the PDF at the printed width, width = mm / 25.4, and set text and lines in points: pointsize, cex, lwd = pt / 0.75.
Check the technical requirements with a script that measures the PDF, and readability by looking at the figure.
An agent can match a picture of a figure closely and still miss a rule by a fraction of a point, which a measurement of the PDF finds.
Matching a picture types every number into the script, and each run types different ones.
Write each journal’s rules in a spec file, with the journal’s words. R, the checking script and an agent all read it.
Check a spec file an agent wrote: its values against the quotes, its rule names with the checking script.
Keep one script per figure, with the journal named once at the top.

Text size and line weight, in points (1 pt = 1/72 inch)
Fonts embedded: a copy of each typeface inside the file
A vector file (PDF or EPS, sharp at any zoom), no pictures inside

Readability, judged by looking at the figure:

Can a reader see the main comparison?
Is any text cut off, overlapping, or on top of data?
Do titles and labels say what is shown, with units?
Can every class be told apart, in gray and by a colour-blind reader?
Do the class breaks spread the data across the classes?

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Nature and AER requirements for size, fonts and text
text:
Nature and AER requirements for size, fonts and text








Requirement
Nature’s words
The AER’s words




Width
“Nature’s standard figure sizes are 89 mm wide (single column) and 183 mm wide (double column).”
Not stated


Font
“Lettering should be in a sans-serif typeface, preferably Helvetica or Arial, the same font throughout all figures in the paper.”
Not stated


Text size
“Maximum text size for all other text should be 7 pt; minimum text size should be 5 pt.”
Not stated


Panel labels
“Separate panels in multi-part figures should each be labelled with 8 pt bold, upright (not italic) a, b, c.”
For file names: “use letters for indicating individual panels (e.g., Figure1a.ppt, Figure1b.ppt, Figure1c.ppt, etc.)”


Line weight
“Line weights and strokes should be set between 0.25 and 1 pt at the final size”
Not stated



Pages: Nature, final submission and preparing figures; AER style guide. Not stated: the rule is yours to set, once for the whole paper.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Nature and AER requirements for files, colour and labels
text:
Nature and AER requirements for files, colour and labels








Requirement
Nature’s words
The AER’s words




File format
“Vector EPS or PDF format for figures containing line drawings and graphs”; “Embed fonts (True Type 2 or 42)”
“Figures must be supplied as vector-based graphics in one of the following formats—vector PDF, EPS, AI, WMF, or PPT.”


Photographs and images
“All photographic images must be supplied at a minimum of 300 dpi at the maximum size they can be used.”
“Photographs and other images (maps, screenshots, etc.) should be provided at 300 dpi”


Colour
“Colour artwork can be provided in RGB (recommended) or CMYK format.”; “An accessible colour palette to be used”
Not stated


Labels
“All axes to be labelled with units in parentheses, e.g. Data (unit)”
“If there are variables (italics) or matrices and vectors (boldface) in figures, they should be designated as such.”



Pages: Nature, final submission and preparing figures; AER style guide. The AER also asks that the files “correspond to the figures in your accompanying PDF”.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: When journals ask for the final figure files
text:
When journals ask for the final figure files

Nature: “The Nature journals are flexible with regard to the format of initial submissions.” “If revisions are requested, the editor will provide detailed formatting instructions at that time.”
AER: “Adherence to the journal’s Style Guide is required for accepted articles but is optional at the time of submission.”
PNAS: each figure as a separate high-quality PDF or EPS file, with the revised manuscript.
Journals ask for the final files at revision (Nature, PNAS) or at acceptance (AER). With the journal’s rules in a file and a figure script that reads them (Part 3), the final files are one run of the script.

Pages: Nature, initial submission; AER, submissions; PNAS, how to submit a manuscript.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: What studies show about presentation and referees
text:
What studies show about presentation and referees


An experiment on writing: Feld, Lines and Ross (JEBO, 2024)

Professional editors improved the English of 30 economics papers, with the layout unchanged.
Economists rated the edited versions 0.2 SD higher and were 8.4 percentage points more likely to accept them for a conference.

Referees’ reasons for rejecting: Bordage (Acad Med, 2001)

On 123 conference submissions that at least one reviewer wanted to reject, text difficult to follow and defective tables or figures were among the ten most common reasons.

A format rule and authors: Card and DellaVigna (JEP, 2014)

After the AER capped submissions at 40 pages in 2008, 21% came in at 39 or 40 pages, up from 6%.

The look of the page: Huang (arXiv, 2018)

A model that saw only page images of computer-vision papers flagged half of the workshop papers (a stand-in for rejected ones) and 0.4% of the conference papers. Referees were not part of the test.



Takeaway: clear writing and readable figures help a paper with referees. No study has sent the same paper to referees in the journal’s format and in a plain one.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
Matching Nature’s requirements in R
Draw the file at the size it will print. Then every size you set is the size the reader sees.







Nature requires
Setting in R




89 mm wide, one column (183 mm for two)
cairo_pdf(width = 89 / 25.4): R takes inches


Helvetica or Arial, embedded in the file
family = "Helvetica"; cairo_pdf() embeds the font


Text from 5 to 7 pt
pointsize = 7 for 7-pt text; cex.axis = 6 / 7 for 6-pt tick labels (printed size = pointsize × cex)


Panel letters, 8 pt bold
mtext("a", font = 2, cex = 8 / 7)


Lines from 0.25 to 1 pt
lwd = 0.5 / 0.75 for a 0.5-pt line (lwd = 1 is 0.75 pt)


A vector file
cairo_pdf() writes one



Point (pt): a length, 1/72 inch or about 0.35 mm; a font’s size in points is the height from the top of an h to the bottom of a p. With layout() or mfrow and three or more rows or columns, R multiplies every text size by 0.66 (0.83 for two by two): add par(cex = 1) after it.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: One Nature column, drawn in the R Console
text:
One Nature column, drawn in the R Console




R Console: writes cars-nature.pdf

# cars comes with R: speed (mph) and
# stopping distance (ft) of 50 cars
cairo_pdf("cars-nature.pdf",
          width = 89 / 25.4, height = 70 / 25.4,
          pointsize = 7, family = "Helvetica")
par(mar = c(3, 3.2, 1.6, 0.6), mgp = c(1.8, 0.5, 0),
    cex.axis = 6 / 7,  # 6-pt tick labels
    lwd = 0.5 / 0.75,  # 0.5-pt box; axes 0.75 pt
    las = 1)
plot(cars$speed, cars$dist, pch = 16, cex = 0.5,
     xlab = "Speed (mph)",
     ylab = "Stopping distance (ft)")
mtext("a", side = 3, line = 0.4, adj = 0,
      font = 2, cex = 8 / 7)   # 8-pt bold letter
dev.off()



The PDF, 89 × 70 mm.


The width, font, text sizes and line weight come from the table on the previous slide.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Categorical, sequential and diverging colour scales
text:
Categorical, sequential and diverging colour scales


Deuteranopia: red–green colour blindness. The eye lacks the cones that sense green, so reds and greens look alike.

“About 1 in 12 men have color vision deficiency”, most often red and green (National Eye Institute). Okabe-Ito colours: Wong (Nature Methods, 2011), the paper Nature’s guide cites. Simulation: Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (IEEE TVCG, 2009), full severity.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
What matching a picture costs

Every number is typed into the script: the page size, the text sizes, the colours, and positions measured in the picture’s pixels.
Some numbers are guesses: the titles came out up to 0.35 pt over Nature’s limit, the panel letters 0.65 pt short.
The same prompt gives different numbers on each run.
The next figure in the paper needs the same work again.
A second journal needs a new target picture and another run.
Nothing in the script says where a number came from.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Why write the requirements in a file
text:
Why write the requirements in a file

In Part 2 the agent had only a picture, so it guessed the sizes. With the rules in a file, it reads them.
The file is specs/nature.yml, a short text file of Nature’s requirements: widths, fonts, text sizes, panel labels, line weights.
Each requirement carries the journal’s own words and the page they come from. We call the file the spec, short for specification.
Three programs read it:

R, to set the size and fonts when it draws
The checking script, tools/check_fig.R, to measure the PDF
Claude Code, when it writes or edits figure code

Edit a value in the file, and every figure drawn after that uses the new value.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
What a YAML file is


What it is: a plain-text file of settings, one name: value per line, ending in .yml or .yaml.

Indenting by two spaces puts a value inside the name above it.
{min: 5, max: 7} is the one-line form of min: 5 and max: 7 indented under the name.
A # after a space starts a comment.
Text with a colon followed by a space goes in quotes.

What uses it: settings that a person writes and a program reads.

The header at the top of a Quarto document, and _quarto.yml
GitHub’s automated jobs (.github/workflows/)

What reads it: Quarto and GitHub, for their own settings · R, with the yaml package · Python, with PyYAML · an agent, as text




R Console; needs the yaml package (install.packages("yaml"))

library(yaml)
s <- read_yaml(text = "
text_pt:
  value: {min: 5, max: 7}
")
s$text_pt$value$max      # a list inside a list
#> [1] 7

title: 12 · Publication graphics
text:
The spec file for Nature


specs/nature.yml (part)

text_pt:
  value: {min: 5, max: 7}
  quote: "Maximum text size for all other text should be 7 pt; minimum text size should be 5 pt."
  source: final

panel_label:
  value: {pt: 8, bold: true, case: lower, placement: inside}
  quote: "Separate panels in multi-part figures should each be labelled with 8 pt bold, upright (not italic) a, b, c."
  source: final (size, bold, lower case); house (letter at top left)

line_pt:
  value: {min: 0.25, max: 1}
  quote: "Line weights and strokes should be set between 0.25 and 1 pt at the
    final size (lines thinner than 0.25 pt may vanish in print)."
  source: final



Each rule has three parts:

value: what R and the checking script use
quote: Nature’s sentence, word for word
source: the page, listed under pages: at the top of the file, or house for our own choice where the pages say nothing

This file comes with the project, with each quote checked against Nature’s pages.
Later in this part, live, Claude Code writes it again from Nature’s pages.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: A script that checks a PDF against the spec file
text:
A script that checks a PDF against the spec file


With Nature’s rules in a file, a script can measure any PDF against them.
tools/check_fig.R reads specs/<journal>.yml, measures the PDF, and prints one line per rule: PASS or FAIL, and what it measured.
It works on any PDF figure, drawn in R, Python or anything else, for any journal with a spec file.
It checks the rules the spec sets as numbers:

Width and height, fonts and whether they are embedded
Text sizes and panel letters
Line weights, and pictures pasted inside the PDF

Readability is left to a person, or to an agent that looks at the figure.
It comes in the project zip, in tools/, written with Claude Code before class: 137 lines of R.
It needs poppler, a free set of command-line tools that read PDFs (on a Mac, brew install poppler), and the R packages yaml and magick.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Asking Claude Code for a checking script
text:
Asking Claude Code for a checking script


Prompt to paste into Claude Code, in a folder with specs/ and some PDFs (a test run, before class)

specs/nature.yml and specs/aer.yml hold two journals' rules for figures,
each with the journal's words. Write tools/check_fig.R, an R script run as
  Rscript tools/check_fig.R <pdf> <journal>
that measures the PDF against specs/<journal>.yml and prints one line per
rule, PASS or FAIL, with what it measured: the page width and height
(pdfinfo), the fonts and whether each is embedded (pdffonts), the size of
every word of text (pdftotext -bbox), the panel letters, and the line
weights (pdftocairo -svg). Read every number from the spec file; type none
into the script. Test it on the PDFs in pdfs/. pdfs/cars-nature.pdf was
drawn 89 x 70 mm with 7-pt text, 6-pt tick labels, an 8-pt bold letter a
and 0.5-pt lines, with embedded fonts, so it should pass every Nature rule.


A test run before class took about 8 minutes and wrote a 461-line script, a different file from the project’s 137-line checker.
On Claude Code’s Part 2 figure it found the same two failures as the project’s script. It passed the target.
On the default figure, which has no panel letters, it printed PASS for the letters (“single panel?”). The project’s script prints FAIL.
Takeaway: test a checker an agent wrote on PDFs whose right answers you know.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: How the checking script measures the width
text:
How the checking script measures the width


Terminal, in the project folder: the tool the script runs for the width

pdfinfo figures/default/figure1.pdf



Output (one line of it)

Page size:       504 x 504 pts



504 pt × 25.4 / 72 = 177.8 mm. The spec allows 89, 120 or 183 mm (one column, a column and a half, two columns), so the width fails.
The other checks follow the same steps, with other tools that read the PDF:

pdffonts: each font, and whether it is embedded
pdftotext -bbox: a box around every word; its height is the text size
pdftocairo -svg: every line, with its width in points

The script runs these tools and compares each result with Nature’s number.


Text sizes are exact for embedded fonts and read about half a point low for fonts that are not embedded.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: The spec file for the AER
text:
The spec file for the AER


specs/aer.yml (part)

panel_label:
  value: {placement: title}
  quote: "Be sure to label your figure files clearly, taking special care to use
    letters for indicating individual panels (e.g., Figure1a.ppt, Figure1b.ppt,
    Figure1c.ppt, etc.)."
  source: style (letters in file names); house ("Panel A." in the title)

width_mm:
  value: {panel: 115}
  quote: not stated
  source: house

text_pt:
  value: {min: 7, max: 9}
  quote: not stated
  source: house

House rule: one the journal does not set, chosen once for the whole paper and marked source: house. The AER’s style guide sets the file format, letters in the names of panel files, and where source notes go. Our house rules: one file per panel, “Panel A.” in the title, panels 115 mm wide, text 7 to 9 pt, lines 0.5 to 1.5 pt, colours that stay distinct in gray.

title: 12 · Publication graphics
section: Live demo: Claude Code rewrites the script to read the spec files
text:
Live demo: Claude Code rewrites the script to read the spec files


Prompt to paste into Claude Code, in match/, after copying the project's specs/ into it

code/figure1_default.R draws Figure 1 for Nature, with every width, font,
text size and line weight typed into the script. specs/nature.yml and
specs/aer.yml hold each journal's rules, with the journal's words.
1. Write R/fig_style.R with three functions: read_spec(journal), which
   reads specs/<journal>.yml; open_fig(), which opens a PDF at the
   journal's width with its font, text size and line weight; and a
   function that draws a panel's label the way the journal asks.
2. Copy the script to code/figure1.R and change it so that
   journal <- "nature" at the top picks the spec, and the script itself
   types no width, font, text size or line weight. For the AER, write one
   file per panel, as specs/aer.yml says.
3. Run it for both journals and check the PDFs with pdfinfo and pdffonts.
