title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Explain what Claude Code has in front of it that a chat window does not: every file in the folder, a terminal, git, and a file of standing instructions, CLAUDE.md.
Start Claude Code in manual mode in an empty RStudio project and have it initialize the git repository.
Hand the tool one task at a time, with a number you counted yourself on the web page it reads; let it run the script; compare.
Read the box that shows each edit, and git diff, before accepting it, and say where every value in the result came from.
Write a CLAUDE.md for the project and a read-only reviewer agent, and say what each one changes.


Five things, and you do each of them on your own laptop as we go.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Plan for today

Chat, Cowork, Claude Code: one model, three harnesses
What you decide and what it does
A project from an empty folder: launch, git, a web page read into a table
Two more columns: is it a postdoc, and in which country
Where the countries came from
CLAUDE.md: the project’s standing instructions
A read-only reviewer agent
Tasks not to give it; practice


The projector shows the instructor’s terminal. Every prompt is on a slide, paste-ready; every result on a slide is from the captured run, so a laptop that falls behind can read what came back.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Chat, Cowork, Claude Code: one model, three harnesses
text:
Chat, Cowork, Claude Code: one model, three harnesses










Chat
Cowork
Claude Code




Where it runs
a web page
the desktop app
your terminal, in one folder


How context arrives
you paste or attach it
from the folder you connect
from the folder, plus a file of standing instructions


Reads your files
no
every file in the folder
every file in the repository


Edits your files
no; you paste its output
yes, directly
yes; each edit shown as a diff first


Runs commands
on Anthropic’s servers, on an attached file
on Anthropic’s servers
on your laptop: R, git, anything in the terminal


Runs your R script
no; you run it
no; you run it
it can, when the prompt says so


What you read afterwards
the script you pasted
git status, git diff
the box that shows each edit, then git diff




Same model in all three. The app around it, the harness, decides what it can see and do. The last column is the only one that acts on your laptop, which is why it asks first and why git is the safety net.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: How Claude Code works: the loop inside the tool
text:
How Claude Code works: the loop inside the tool






It picks a tool: read, search, run a command, edit a file. The result comes back to it. Again, until done.
Manual mode, today’s setting: an edit, or a command that changes something, asks you first. Reading never asks.
A session starts empty. What carries over is on disk: files, commits, CLAUDE.md.


The model writes text only. Every read, run and edit is a request the harness carries out and reports back. In manual mode the requests that change something come to you as approval boxes.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: What changes when a tool can edit your files
text:
What changes when a tool can edit your files

It can read any file in the repository. Nothing private goes in that folder.
Its edits land on disk, not in a chat.
It can run commands, including git.
It shows every edit as a diff before it lands. You accept or refuse.
Anything it reads goes to Anthropic’s servers. Restricted data stays out; develop on a public or synthetic sample.
What is right is still your call.


Each of these needs a habit; git and reading the diff are the two.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: You decide the question; it writes the code
text:
You decide the question; it writes the code

It is strong at writing, refactoring and debugging code. It is weak at judging whether a specification answers your question.
Decide the estimand, the sample, the weights, the fixed effects and the clustering yourself. Then ask it to implement them.
Let it choose and it picks something plausible. Plausible is not the same as right.
A fact it did not read is a guess: a function’s arguments, a citation, a fact about the world. Check the documentation, the paper, the source.
You must be able to explain every line. Ask it to explain rather than write, and it becomes a tutor.


Treat it as a fast, capable research assistant that needs clear instructions and close supervision. The third bullet is today’s project: a country column.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: The main risk is silent errors, not crashes
text:
The main risk is silent errors, not crashes

Code that fails is easy to fix. Code that runs and is wrong is the danger.
The usual shapes: a merge that drops or duplicates rows; NAs handled silently; a unit mismatch; an estimation call that differs a little from what you asked.
Three defenses: explicit checks, stopifnot() on row counts, unique keys and value ranges; estimators tried on simulated data with known parameters; the merge and the regression call read by you.
Git is the safety net: commit before each task, read the diff after it, git restore puts a file back.


Every defense is something you do. The tool can write the check; it cannot decide what the right row count is.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Small tasks, short sessions, a plan before code
text:
Small tasks, short sessions, a plan before code

One well-defined task per session: “build the county-year panel”, “write the event-study plot”. “Do the analysis” produces large vague code.
Performance drops as the context fills with old material. Start a fresh conversation between unrelated tasks (the /clear command).
Anything with a merge or a panel build: “Describe your approach before writing any code.” Read the plan; fix misunderstandings there, where they are cheap.
Conventions you would otherwise repeat go once into CLAUDE.md, a file it reads at every launch: base R only, never touch data/raw/, relative paths, a clean session, a master script, seeds, sessionInfo() saved with results.


Plan mode exists for the third bullet; the sentence works in any mode. CLAUDE.md is the sixth part of today.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Two rules: a clean git state, and the diff over the transcript
text:
Two rules: a clean git state, and the diff over the transcript

Start from a clean git state. git status clean before the prompt; afterwards the diff is exactly what the model did.
Trust the diff, not the transcript. What it did, not what its replies say it did.
Commit before each task; read every diff before you commit; git restore puts a file back.


Rule one is why rule two works. A dirty tree mixes your edits with its edits, and the diff no longer shows what the model did. The diff-reading habit from the git session is the whole reason rule two is usable.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: The project: the Ph.D. placements page, from an empty folder
text:
The project: the Ph.D. placements page, from an empty folder

The page: Recent job placements, Ph.D. in Applied Economics & Management. One table: year, name, position, organization. 109 rows when captured.
Four prompts, one task each: 1 start git; 2 read the table into a CSV (scraping); 3 flag the postdocs; 4 add each organization’s country. Then: where the countries came from.
The prompts tell the tool to run the script and fix it when it fails. You check every number against the page.
The folder: placements, no git yet. Once, in the Console: install.packages("rvest"), the R package that reads web pages.


A public page, one table, and a column the page does not have. The instructor’s terminal is on the projector; the slides carry the prompts and what came back.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: The steps, from an empty folder to the first prompt
text:
The steps, from an empty folder to the first prompt

RStudio: File → New Project → New Directory → New Project. Name placements, inside ~/github. Do not tick Create a git repository. Create Project.
Console, once: install.packages("rvest").
Tools → Terminal → New Terminal. The prompt ends in placements.
Type claude --permission-mode manual, Enter.
The trust question: ↓ once to Yes, I trust this folder, Enter.
The welcome screen: the folder ends in placements; the status line reads ⏸ manual mode on.
Ask it to set up git, in these words: “Initialize a git repository in this folder, add a .gitignore for an RStudio project, and commit everything.” Read each box, 1. Yes.
Tools → Terminal → New Terminal again (Terminal 2): git log --oneline.


Eight steps, one slide each from here on. Step 7 is the exact sentence, short; the full prompt, with the file names and the commit message, is five slides on. Nobody types ahead: we do them together, and everyone gets to step 8 before Prompt 2.
When it fails, say:

command not found: claude: Before class step 2; quit and reopen RStudio; pair up for now.
The Terminal shows R’s > prompt instead of ❯: they typed claude in the Console. Tools → Terminal → New Terminal, then again.
The status line says auto mode: /exit, then claude --permission-mode manual.
The trust question again: the terminal is outside the project; Tools → Terminal → New Terminal from inside it.
there is no package called 'rvest': install.packages("rvest") in the Console; then tell the tool to run again.
No Bash box for git and the reply says it cannot run commands: the status line is not manual, or the folder was not trusted; /exit, relaunch, look at the status line.
The box never appears and it prints code instead: it wrote nothing; ask again with the artifact line, “Write code/placements.R”, first.
The row count differs from the page: the page changed since capture; the count for one year is the check that matters.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Claude Code in RStudio’s Terminal tab
text:
Claude Code in RStudio’s Terminal tab





Terminal tab: where Claude Code runs
❯ prompt: where you type
Console: where you run the script
Files pane: what it wrote



It runs in the Terminal tab, inside the project, so the paths are the project’s paths. The Console stays free for running the script. This is the same tab they used for git; say so here, not on the page.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Launching Claude Code in manual mode
text:
Launching Claude Code in manual mode
claude --permission-mode manual

Manual mode: it asks before every edit and every command that changes something.
The status line must read ⏸ manual mode on.
Any other mode: /exit, then this line again.


Use this line, not bare claude, until reading diffs is a habit.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
The trust question





The path: must end in placements
No, exit is highlighted
↓ once, then Enter
Asked once per folder



Read the path before you press anything. If it is your home folder, you are about to trust a tool with everything in it. The screen is from another folder; yours ends in placements.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Reading the welcome screen





Version: the number varies; any current one
Model · plan: the model in use and your plan; wording varies
Folder: ends in placements
❯: type here, Enter sends
Status line: ⏸ manual mode on



Line three and the status line. If either is wrong, exit and relaunch; nothing else on this screen matters yet.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Keys, commands, and a second Terminal tab
text:
Keys, commands, and a second Terminal tab



Key or command
Does




Enter
sends the prompt


Esc
interrupts; on a question, declines


↑
brings back the previous prompt


/clear
new conversation, same folder


/exit (or Ctrl+C twice)
leaves Claude Code


Tools → Terminal → New Terminal
a second tab for git




Esc interrupts whatever it is doing. Open a second Terminal tab for git, so you can read what it did without leaving the tool.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Prompt 1: git, from inside the tool
text:
Prompt 1: git, from inside the tool


Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)

Initialize a git repository in this folder, add a .gitignore for an RStudio
project (.Rproj.user, .Rhistory, .RData), and commit everything with the
message "New project".






A box shows the new file .gitignore first: read it, 1. Yes
A box shows the exact git command: read it, 1. Yes
Terminal 2: git log --oneline prints one commit



The box is from another project; the shape is the same. Two boxes today: a file and a command. Auto mode would have asked for neither. Its commit message carries a Co-Authored-By line naming the model.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: One task per prompt: the four parts
text:
One task per prompt: the four parts

The goal: what the script must do, with names for its inputs and its output.
The mistake to avoid, named: the plausible wrong reading. Call it the failure mode.
The file to write, and where: code/<name>.R.
What not to do: no other files; no git, so that you read the diff and commit; and whether to run the script.
Prompt 1 had three of the four; Prompt 2, the scraper, has all four. Paste them; do not retype them.


Part two is the one novices leave out. Prompt 4, the country column, is what happens without it.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: How much to ask for in one prompt: one task, one file
text:
How much to ask for in one prompt: one task, one file







Too big to check
Right-sized




“Do my analysis of the placements.”
“Write code/placements.R: the table on the placements page, saved as data/placements.csv, four columns.”


“Make a report on placements.”
“Add a column postdoc: TRUE when the position is a postdoc. Change nothing else.”


“Fix my script.”
“The 2015 rows are missing; change the line that filters the years, nothing else.”




The test: name one number the answer must contain, and work that number out yourself, before you send the prompt.
For the scraper, next slide: the page shows 16 rows for 2026, and you can count them. So the task is small enough to check.
No such number: the request is too big. Split it.


“Do my analysis” has no number in it, so there is nothing to compare afterwards. A big job is several small ones in a row, each checked before the next.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Three questions before you send a prompt
text:
Three questions before you send a prompt

Can you say in advance what a wrong answer would look like, and write that into the prompt?
Can you work out one number of the answer yourself, from the page or from rows on your screen?
Could you read the whole diff in five minutes?


Any no: the task is too big. Split it and send the first part.


For the scraper: a wrong answer is rows dropped or doubled, or the other table on the page; the number is 16 rows for 2026; the diff is one new file of about thirty lines. Three yes, so it goes.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
The five-step delegation loop






Next: the table read from the page. The count on paper: one year’s rows, counted on the page.
Then two columns, each with its own count.
The permanent check: the counts written into the script, dated.


Step three is the one people skip. Without a value on paper, step four is only watching a script run.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Prompt 2: the scraper, run until it works
text:
Prompt 2: the scraper, run until it works


Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)

Write code/placements.R. It reads the table "Recent job placements" at
https://business.cornell.edu/admissions/graduate/phd-aem/for-hire/ and saves
it as data/placements.csv with the page's four columns, year, name, position,
organization, one row per graduate. Use the rvest package for the HTML and
base R for the rest. Run it with Rscript code/placements.R; if it fails, fix
the script and run again. Then show me the first five rows and the number of
rows. Do not use git.


It looked at the page’s two tables first (two Bash command boxes), then Create file, then Rscript.
What came back: “Wrote 109 rows”, the first five rows, how it chose the table.
Your check, on the page: count the 2026 rows. 16. Console: sum(read.csv("data/placements.csv")$year == 2026).
“Do not use git”: a commit made for you is a diff you never read. From here, you commit.


The last clause is the one to explain out loud: a commit made for you is a diff you never read. Prompt 1 was the exception, and we watched that command before it ran.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: The approval box for a new file
text:
The approval box for a new file





Create file, and the path
The file, every line
1. Yes: Enter writes it
2.: stops asking about edits. Leave it.
3. No or Esc: refuse



The box is from another project; the shape is the same. Read the file before it exists. Today: which lines pick the table?

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: git diff --staged on the scraper: the lines to read
text:
git diff --staged on the scraper: the lines to read
git add code/placements.R
git diff --staged
wanted  <- c("year", "name", "position", "organization")
headers <- lapply(tables, function(tb) tolower(html_text2(html_elements(tb, "th"))))
hit     <- which(vapply(headers, function(h) identical(h, wanted), logical(1)))
if (length(hit) != 1) {
  stop("Expected exactly one placements table with columns ", ...)
}

A new file: every line is a +. Read it top to bottom once.
These lines matter: it picks the table by its header, not by its position, and stops if there is not exactly one.
A line you cannot explain: ask for an explanation before you accept. vapply() and identical() are two to ask about.


The transcript said how it chose the table; the diff shows it. Now you have read it rather than been told it.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: How to judge a model’s diff: five questions
text:
How to judge a model’s diff: five questions

Which files changed? Only the ones you named? (git status)
What was deleted? Read the red lines first. Did you ask for each one to go?
Which line does the actual work? Does it do what you asked, and nothing more?
Where does each value in it come from? Your data, or typed into the code by the tool?
Is there a line you could not explain to someone? Ask what it does before you accept it.


Five questions, in this order. The second one is where an unasked change hides.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Prompt 3: a postdoc flag


Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)

Add a column postdoc to the table before it is saved: TRUE when the position
is a postdoc, FALSE otherwise. Change nothing else. Run it again and tell me
how many rows are TRUE.

+# Flag postdoc positions; spellings on the page include "Postdoc", "Post-doc",
+# "Post Doctoral Fellow" and "Postdoctoral Associate".
+placements$postdoc <- grepl("post[- ]?doc", placements$position, ignore.case = TRUE)

It looked at the spellings first: eleven of them. One pattern covers the three shapes: joined, hyphen, space.
25 of 109 rows are TRUE. One judgment call in its reply: a row listed as both a postdoc and an assistant professor.
The hand check, Ctrl+F on the page: “postdoc” 15, “post-doc” 9, “post doc” 1. 25.


The edit box shows one comment and one line. A pattern you cannot read is question 5: ask it to explain [- ]?.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: The approval box for an edit: red and green lines
text:
The approval box for an edit: red and green lines





- red: what goes. Read these first.
+ green: what arrives
Line 1: changed unasked; harmless, but read it
1. Yes accepts; Esc refuses



The box is from another project; the shape is the same. Two red lines where one was asked for: the extra one is a comment. Notice it, then accept it. The country edit has no red lines and thirty green ones.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Your own check, typed into the script and committed with it
text:
Your own check, typed into the script and committed with it
 placements$postdoc <- grepl("post[- ]?doc", placements$position, ignore.case = TRUE)
+
+# Counted on the page on 2026-09-21: 16 rows for 2026; postdoc spellings
+# 15 + 9 + 1. When the page changes this stops the script: recount, then edit.
+stopifnot(sum(placements$year == 2026) == 16, sum(placements$postdoc) == 25)

Your two counts, 16 and 25, as one line the script must satisfy every run. You type it, not the tool.
Committed with the code, so the check travels with the script.
If the page changes or a later edit breaks the scraper, the script stops here instead of writing a wrong CSV.


This is the answer to “how would you ever notice”. Say it plainly: you checked once by hand, and now the script does that check on every run, for good, because it is in the file and in the commit.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Prompt 4: a country column


Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)

Add a column country with the country of the organization. Change nothing
else. Run it again and show me the number of rows per country.



What it printed after running the script again

United States 77   China 7   India 4   Australia 3   Canada 3
Germany 2   Hong Kong 2   Singapore 2   Finland 1   France 1
New Zealand 1   Norway 1   Saudi Arabia 1   South Korea 1
Switzerland 1   Vietnam 1   Zambia 1


It added the column, ran the script, and printed the counts. 109 rows, 17 countries, no error.
Its reply ends: the assignments “all look right”.
Before you accept it: open the diff and read the new lines. The next slide is that diff.


Say nothing yet about how it got the countries. Let them look at the diff on the next slide and answer question 4 themselves.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: The diff for the country column: where does each value come from?
text:
The diff for the country column: where does each value come from?
country_patterns <- c(
  "Australia"    = "Monash|New South Wales|University of Sydney",
  "Canada"       = "Alberta|Calgary|Ottawa",
  "China"        = "Beijing|Peking|Renmin|Xi.an Jiaotong",
  "Germany"      = "Ludwig-Maximilian|DTUM",
  ...                                        # sixteen countries in all
)
placements$country <- "United States"
for (ctry in names(country_patterns)) { ... }

Question 4, on this diff: for each value the column can take, where did it come from?
"Australia", "Canada", "China", and thirteen more: typed here.
"United States": typed here too, and given to every row that matches nothing. That is 77 of the 109.


Give them a minute on the code before the next slide. Ask the room: which of these seventeen countries is written anywhere on the page they scraped? The answer is on the next slide.
When it fails, say:

The pattern matched fewer than the page count: it matched one spelling; the check would have caught it; ask for a patch naming the missing spelling.
No country table, it wrote NA for everything: a better run than the captured one; read its reply for why, and go to step 5 anyway.
It asked to fetch the organizations’ web pages: Esc; that is a different task, and today the facts are yours to supply.
git diff shows the postdoc line removed: “Change nothing else” was not held; git restore code/placements.R and ask again.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Where the countries came from

The page names a place for 14 of 109 rows. Nothing else on the page says a country.
The rest is memory: a table it typed, and a default. It said so, in a comment and in its reply, and the column still went into the CSV.
DTUM: Denmark in one run, Germany in the next. Same prompt, same page.
Plausible is not the same as right. A fact it did not read is a guess, however confident the sentence around it.
The script ran without error both times.


Two runs on the same evening. Ask the room which one is right. Nobody in the room knows, and that is the answer: it is not data.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: What would have caught it earlier
text:
What would have caught it earlier

A plan before code. “Describe your approach before writing any code.” The captured reply proposes a lookup table it would “populate myself from knowledge of the institutions” and mark “the handful I’m unsure about”. You read that and say no.
Question 4 of the five, asked of the diff. Where does each value come from? Sixteen country names sit in the code, and none of them came from the page or from you.
A reviewer with fresh eyes. A second Claude that never saw this conversation, later today, found it in one turn.


All three are cheap. The plan costs one sentence in the prompt and one minute of reading.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Prompt 5, the fix: facts you supply live in a data file
text:
Prompt 5, the fix: facts you supply live in a data file


Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)

The page does not state countries, so the lookup is a guess. Replace it: write
the distinct organizations to data/countries.csv with an empty country column
for me to fill in, read that file in the script, and set country to NA when
the organization is not in it or its country is empty. Change nothing else.
Run it and tell me how many rows have NA.

countries <- read.csv(file.path("data", "countries.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
countries$country[trimws(countries$country) == ""] <- NA
placements$country <- countries$country[match(placements$organization,
                                              countries$organization)]

data/countries.csv: 107 organizations, an empty country column, written once.
109 of 109 rows are NA until you fill it. The CSV claims nothing nobody checked.
Fill ten rows from the organizations’ pages, run, commit the file.


The tool did the plumbing: the file, the match, the NA. The facts are yours to type, and git records that you typed them.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: CLAUDE.md: standing instructions, read at every launch
text:
CLAUDE.md: standing instructions, read at every launch

A markdown file at the root, read at every launch.
Layout, style, facts and checks, working rules. Nothing that changes per task.
Short: 35 lines here. The docs’ target is under 200.
Committed. It is part of the record.


Everything you would otherwise paste into every prompt, written once.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
/init: a first draft of CLAUDE.md





This project has none. Nothing made one for you.
/init reads the folder, writes a first draft.
The same box as any new file: 1. Yes.
A draft of what it found, not of how you want code written.



A starting point from what it saw. What it did not see is how you want code written.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
The CLAUDE.md for placements


CLAUDE.md (excerpt; the full file is on the page)

# placements
## Style
- Base R. The only package is `rvest`, and only for reading HTML.
- A number or a URL that could change sits at the top of the script as a
  named constant in capitals: `URL <- "..."`.
- Comments say why, not what.
## Facts and checks
- A fact that is not on the page and not in a data file does not go into
  code. Put it in a file under `data/` that I fill in, and use `NA` until
  I do.
- After a merge or a filter, check the row count with `stopifnot()`.
## Working rules
- Do not run scripts unless the prompt asks. I run them in RStudio.
- Do not use git unless the prompt asks. I commit.


Paste it over the draft, save, commit, relaunch. Thirty-five lines. The “Facts and checks” section is this afternoon’s lesson, written down once.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Style habits in CLAUDE.md: naming, structure, constants, comments
text:
Style habits in CLAUDE.md: naming, structure, constants, comments

Naming: snake_case; file names say what the script does.
Structure: one script per task; a function does one job.
Named constants: URL <- "..." at the top, never a bare value below.
Comments say why, not what. A header on every script.
Facts and checks: a fact not on the page goes in a data file; a row count after every merge.
Written once. Read at every launch. Copy it to the next repository.


Your style sheet is how you brief an assistant. It is also how you brief yourself in December. The five habits are the style handout; this is where it pays off.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
A one-sentence prompt after CLAUDE.md


Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)

Write code/by_year.R: for each year, the number of placements and the number
of postdocs, from data/placements.csv, printed as a table with one row per
year.

# Reads data/placements.csv. Writes nothing; prints a table with one row
# per year giving the number of placements and the number of postdocs.

PLACEMENTS <- "data/placements.csv"

count_by_year <- function(placements) {
  ...
  # Every placement belongs to exactly one year, so the counts must add up.
  stopifnot(sum(by_year$n_placements) == nrow(placements))
  by_year
}

Not in the prompt: the header, the constant, the function, the row check, “do not run it”. All in CLAUDE.md.
Its last sentence: “Not run, per the project rules.”


What is missing from the prompt is in the file it read at launch. The check on the counts came from the “Facts and checks” section.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Subagents: a second Claude with its own context
text:
Subagents: a second Claude with its own context

A subagent is a separate conversation the tool starts for one task: its own empty context, its own tool list, CLAUDE.md included. It returns a report, not its working.
When: reading many files, so your context stays small; an independent review of a diff or a rule, so the checker is not the thing being checked.
One line: Use a subagent to review code/x.R against this rule: ... Report what it says. Do not edit anything.
Permanent: a file in .claude/agents/, like CLAUDE.md: a name, a description, the tools it may use, then its instructions.


The reviewer never saw the conversation that wrote the code. That is the point, and it is the same rule as typing the check yourself.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: A read-only reviewer subagent: the file
text:
A read-only reviewer subagent: the file


.claude/agents/hand-check-reviewer.md

---
name: hand-check-reviewer
description: Reviews one R script against one rule from the request. Read-only.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

You review one R script against one rule given in the request. Read the
script. Reply in three lines: the rule; the line of code that follows it
or breaks it, quoted; the verdict, "follows" or "breaks". Do not edit any
file. Do not propose a rewrite unless asked.


Save, commit, relaunch. The name is how you call it.
tools: is the fence: it can read; it cannot edit or run anything.


Same shape as CLAUDE.md: written once, read when called. The body is its standing instructions; the request supplies the rule.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: The reviewer on placements.R: the report
text:
The reviewer on placements.R: the report


Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run, before the fix)

Use the hand-check-reviewer subagent to review code/placements.R against this
rule: every value in the country column must come from the page or from a data
file, never from a table typed into the code. Report what it says. Do not edit
anything.



The subagent's report, condensed; the full report is on the page

Rule: every value in the country column must come from the page or from a
  data file, never from a table typed into the code.
Line that breaks it (code/placements.R, lines 44-67): country_patterns <- c(
  "Australia" = "Monash|New South Wales|University of Sydney", ...) and
  placements$country <- "United States".
No data file is read anywhere; the only input is read_html(url) on line 10.
Verdict: breaks.


One turn, a fresh context, line numbers. Nothing edited: git status is clean.
It found what question 4 finds. The difference: it did not write the code it judged.


Same rule as typing the check yourself: the checker is not the thing being checked.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Tasks not to give Claude Code
text:
Tasks not to give Claude Code

Outputs you cannot check by hand.
Facts it did not read: a country, a citation, a function’s arguments.
Restricted data. It sends what it reads to Anthropic’s servers: develop on a public or synthetic sample, run the final code yourself.
Questions that do not touch the repository. Use a chat.
Long stretches without reading: accept-edits mode, until reading diffs is a habit.


Every one of these is a case where the diff is not enough, or you would not read it.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: A script that runs without error can still be wrong
text:
A script that runs without error can still be wrong

The country script ran without error twice and wrote 109 countries. Fourteen came from the page.
Reading the diff made that visible; a data file you fill keeps it visible; a dated count keeps the scraper honest.
The bottleneck is verification, not typing. A faster tool moves it to where it is easiest to skip.


A clean run is not a right answer.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Practice
Nine exercises on the session page, with solutions behind a click. All of them run in placements, never in a graded repository.

1–2 Read-only prompts: an explanation of the scraper; what a page change would do
3–4 Facts and checks: fill ten countries; a count per organization with a hand check
5–6 Break things on purpose: the pattern; the check; git restore
7–8 CLAUDE.md and the reviewer: add a rule; review by_year.R
9 Your own small project, reorganized under a CLAUDE.md

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Quick reference
Count it on the page before you run it, read the diff before you accept it, and keep facts you supply in a data file.
Every command, key, prompt shape and check from today, one line each, on the session page, with the things that bite.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Slides · Source
How to work with a coding agent in your terminal as a fast research assistant that needs clear instructions and close supervision. The first part says what it has in front of it that a chat window does not, and what you decide before it writes a line. The second part builds a small project from an empty folder: a scraper for the Dyson School’s Ph.D. placements page, a postdoc flag, a country column, and the moment the tool fills a column from memory. The third part writes the project’s CLAUDE.md and a read-only reviewer agent. Every step runs in RStudio’s Terminal tab.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Objectives
By the end of this session you can:

Explain what Claude Code has in front of it that a chat window does not: every file in the folder, a terminal, git, and a file of standing instructions, CLAUDE.md.
Start Claude Code in manual mode in an empty RStudio project and have it initialize the git repository.
Hand the tool one task at a time, with a number you counted yourself on the web page it reads; let it run the script; compare.
Read the box that shows each edit, and git diff, before accepting it, and say where every value in the result came from.
Write a CLAUDE.md for the project and a read-only reviewer agent, and say what each one changes.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Chat, Cowork, Claude Code: one model, three harnesses
text:
Chat, Cowork, Claude Code: one model, three harnesses










Chat
Cowork
Claude Code




Where it runs
a web page
the desktop app
your terminal, in one folder


How context arrives
you paste or attach it
from the folder you connect
from the folder, plus a file of standing instructions


Reads your files
no
every file in the folder
every file in the repository


Edits your files
no; you paste its output
yes, directly
yes; each edit shown as a diff first


Runs commands
on Anthropic’s servers, on an attached file
on Anthropic’s servers
on your laptop: R, git, anything in the terminal


Runs your R script
no; you run it
no; you run it
it can, when the prompt says so


What you read afterwards
the script you pasted
git status, git diff
the box that shows each edit, then git diff



Claude Code is the same Claude model as the chat window and Cowork, in a third harness: a program in your terminal that runs in one folder. The harness decides what the model can see and do. In a chat you paste context in and copy text out. Cowork reads and writes the files in a folder you connect and runs code in a sandbox on Anthropic’s servers, not on your laptop. Claude Code reads every file in the repository, edits files after showing each edit as a diff, and runs commands in your terminal: R, git, anything you could type there. That row is the difference that matters. The other two never touch your machine; this one does, which is why it asks before acting and why git is the safety net.
Two other kinds of tool are not this page’s subject. An inline tool such as GitHub Copilot in RStudio proposes the next few lines in the editor and sees only the open file. Terminal agents from other vendors work like Claude Code; the habits on this page transfer to them.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: How Claude Code works: the loop inside the tool
text:
How Claude Code works: the loop inside the tool



The loop inside the tool. In manual mode, step 3 stops and asks you before an edit or a command that changes something.


Inside the tool runs a loop. Your prompt goes to the model together with a hidden system prompt and, if the folder has one, CLAUDE.md. The model writes text and nothing else; it cannot open a file or run a command itself. So it writes a request for a tool, and the harness carries it out: read a file, search the folder, run a command in the terminal, edit a file. The tool’s result comes back to the model as text, and the model decides the next step. That repeats until nothing is left to do; then you get a reply. Anthropic’s page How Claude Code works describes the same loop in three phases: gather context, take action, verify results. In today’s project the tool runs the script and fixes it when it fails; the third phase is still yours, because only you know the number the script must reproduce.
In manual mode the loop stops at every edit and at every command that changes something and asks you; reading is free. You can stop it too: Esc interrupts. Everything the model has in front of it at a given moment is its context: the system prompt, CLAUDE.md, your prompts, every file it read and every command output so far. A new session starts with an empty context. What carries over is what is on disk: the files, the commits, and CLAUDE.md.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: What changes when a tool can edit your files
text:
What changes when a tool can edit your files

It can read any file in the repository. Nothing private goes in that folder.
Its edits land on disk, not in a chat.
It can run commands, including git.
It shows every edit as a diff before it lands. You accept or refuse.
Anything it reads goes to Anthropic’s servers. Restricted data stays out; develop on a public or synthetic sample.
What is right is still your call.

Four things change. It can read any file in the repository, so what it sees is not what you pasted but what is on disk. Its edits land on disk, not in a chat window. It can run commands, including scripts and git. Every edit appears as a diff before it lands; that diff is the one thing you must read. Anything it reads is sent to Anthropic’s servers for processing, so check your data use agreements before pointing it at confidential files; the practical workaround is to let it develop the code on a synthetic or public sample with the same structure, and to run the final code yourself on the restricted data. The verification is yours; the tool has no way to compare the number it produced with the number you meant.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: You decide the question; it writes the code
text:
You decide the question; it writes the code

It is strong at writing, refactoring and debugging code. It is weak at judging whether a specification answers your question.
Decide the estimand, the sample, the weights, the fixed effects and the clustering yourself. Then ask it to implement them.
Let it choose and it picks something plausible. Plausible is not the same as right.
A fact it did not read is a guess: a function’s arguments, a citation, a fact about the world. Check the documentation, the paper, the source.
You must be able to explain every line. Ask it to explain rather than write, and it becomes a tutor.

Claude Code is most useful when you treat it as a fast, capable research assistant that needs clear instructions and close supervision. It is strong at writing, refactoring and debugging code. It is weaker at judging whether a specification answers your question. So you own the identification and it owns the plumbing: decide the estimand, the fixed effects, the clustering and the sample restrictions yourself, then ask it to implement them. If you let it choose, it will pick something plausible, and plausible is not the same as right.
The same rule covers facts. It can misremember a function’s arguments, especially in less common packages; it can cite papers that do not exist or misstate what they found; it can fill a column with countries it never read anywhere. Check documentation and citations yourself, and treat any value it did not read from your data or your page as a guess until you have checked it. Today’s project shows this with a country column.
For students, understanding comes first. It is possible to produce working code without understanding it. The rule in this course is that you can explain every line of code in your analysis. Ask the tool to explain its code rather than only write it; that turns it into a tutor. A line you still cannot explain after the explanation is a line to replace with one you can.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: The main risk is silent errors, not crashes
text:
The main risk is silent errors, not crashes

Code that fails is easy to fix. Code that runs and is wrong is the danger.
The usual shapes: a merge that drops or duplicates rows; NAs handled silently; a unit mismatch; an estimation call that differs a little from what you asked.
Three defenses: explicit checks, stopifnot() on row counts, unique keys and value ranges; estimators tried on simulated data with known parameters; the merge and the regression call read by you.
Git is the safety net: commit before each task, read the diff after it, git restore puts a file back.

Code that fails is easy to fix: the error names the line. Code that runs but is wrong is the real danger, and it is the common case with a tool that writes plausible code quickly. The usual shapes are a merge that drops or duplicates rows, NAs handled in a way you did not expect, a unit mismatch, and an estimation call that differs slightly from what you asked for: a different standard error, a sample restriction applied one step too late.
Three defenses, all yours. Ask for explicit checks, stopifnot() on row counts after a merge, on unique keys, on value ranges; the tool writes them well once you name the number. Test estimators on simulated data with known parameters before running them on real data; if the estimate does not recover the parameter you planted, the code is wrong, whatever the transcript says. And read the key lines yourself, the merges and the regression call above all.
Git is the safety net around all of it. Commit before each task, so the diff afterwards is exactly what the tool did. Review that diff. Claude Code edits many files quickly, and git is what lets you see what changed and roll back with git restore. If you do not use git yet, this tool is the best reason to start.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Small tasks, short sessions, a plan before code
text:
Small tasks, short sessions, a plan before code

One well-defined task per session: “build the county-year panel”, “write the event-study plot”. “Do the analysis” produces large vague code.
Performance drops as the context fills with old material. Start a fresh conversation between unrelated tasks (the /clear command).
Anything with a merge or a panel build: “Describe your approach before writing any code.” Read the plan; fix misunderstandings there, where they are cheap.
Conventions you would otherwise repeat go once into CLAUDE.md, a file it reads at every launch: base R only, never touch data/raw/, relative paths, a clean session, a master script, seeds, sessionInfo() saved with results.

Keep tasks small and sessions short. Everything the model has in front of it competes for its attention, and performance drops as the context fills with old material. Give one well-defined task per session, such as “build the county-year panel” or “write the event-study plot”, and use /clear between unrelated tasks. Large vague requests like “do the analysis” produce large vague code that nobody can check.
Plan before it writes code. For anything nontrivial, use plan mode (Shift+Tab cycles to it) or simply write “Describe your approach before writing any code.” Read the plan. Fix misunderstandings at that stage, when they are cheap. This habit matters most for data construction steps like merges and panel building, and today’s project shows what it would have caught.
Build reproducibility in from the start, as standing rules rather than reminders: a master script that runs the whole pipeline in order, package versions locked (renv is one way), a seed for anything stochastic, sessionInfo() saved with the results. The tool follows such rules reliably once they are written in CLAUDE.md, the file it reads at the start of every session; the sixth part of this page writes one for the project.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Two rules: a clean git state, and the diff over the transcript
text:
Two rules: a clean git state, and the diff over the transcript

Start from a clean git state. git status clean before the prompt; afterwards the diff is exactly what the model did.
Trust the diff, not the transcript. What it did, not what its replies say it did.
Commit before each task; read every diff before you commit; git restore puts a file back.

Rule one: start from a clean git state. git status prints nothing to commit, working tree clean before you type a prompt; then every line the diff shows afterwards is the model’s, and none is yours. Rule two: trust the diff, not the transcript. The transcript says what the tool claims it did. The diff shows what it did. When they disagree, the diff wins.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: The project: the Ph.D. placements page, from an empty folder
text:
The project: the Ph.D. placements page, from an empty folder

The page: Recent job placements, Ph.D. in Applied Economics & Management. One table: year, name, position, organization. 109 rows when captured.
Four prompts, one task each: 1 start git; 2 read the table into a CSV (scraping); 3 flag the postdocs; 4 add each organization’s country. Then: where the countries came from.
The prompts tell the tool to run the script and fix it when it fails. You check every number against the page.
The folder: placements, no git yet. Once, in the Console: install.packages("rvest"), the R package that reads web pages.

The project is small and real. The Dyson School lists its recent Ph.D. placements on one public page as a table with four columns: year, name, position, organization. We scrape it into a CSV, add a column that flags postdocs, and add a column with the country of each organization. The page does not state the country, and that is the point of the third prompt.
Two things differ from a chat. The prompts tell the tool to run the script and fix it when it fails, so the tool is the loop; your job is the check, a number you count on the page before you believe the number on the screen. And everything starts from an empty folder: no repository, no script, nothing the tool did not write in front of you.
Every prompt on this page is the exact text of one captured run on 2026-09-21, and every number is from that run: 109 rows, 16 of them in 2026, 25 postdocs. The page grows every year, so the numbers on your screen will differ. The prompts, the checks and the lesson do not.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: The steps, from an empty folder to the first prompt
text:
The steps, from an empty folder to the first prompt

RStudio: File → New Project → New Directory → New Project. Name placements, inside ~/github. Do not tick Create a git repository. Create Project.
Console, once: install.packages("rvest").
Tools → Terminal → New Terminal. The prompt ends in placements.
Type claude --permission-mode manual, Enter.
The trust question: ↓ once to Yes, I trust this folder, Enter.
The welcome screen: the folder ends in placements; the status line reads ⏸ manual mode on.
Ask it to set up git, in these words: “Initialize a git repository in this folder, add a .gitignore for an RStudio project, and commit everything.” Read each box, 1. Yes.
Tools → Terminal → New Terminal again (Terminal 2): git log --oneline.

The whole path, in order; the next six sections take the steps one at a time. The RStudio project is the folder: New Project creates ~/github/placements with one file in it, placements.Rproj, and every Terminal you open from Tools → Terminal starts there, so there is nothing to navigate. Leave the git box unticked: the first prompt asks the tool to do that part, and you watch it happen. If you did Before class, steps 1 and 2 are done; open the project (File → Recent Projects → placements) and start at step 3.
Everything on this page also works without RStudio, in a plain terminal or in VS Code; the slides show the RStudio path because that is where the course runs R.






NoteThe same steps in a plain terminal, or in VS Code





A plain terminal (Terminal on a Mac, PowerShell on Windows):
mkdir -p ~/github/placements
cd ~/github/placements
claude --permission-mode manual
Then the trust question, the welcome screen and the first prompt as on the slides. Git goes in a second terminal window opened in the same folder (cd ~/github/placements, then git log --oneline or git diff). Run a script with Rscript code/placements.R from that folder, or open the folder in RStudio when you want the Console.
VS Code: File → Open Folder → placements. View → Terminal opens a terminal in that folder; type claude --permission-mode manual there. The + button on the terminal panel opens a second terminal for git. To read what changed, open the Source Control view (the branch icon in the left bar): it lists every changed file, and clicking one opens the diff side by side, the same lines git diff prints. Anthropic also ships a Claude Code extension for VS Code that shows each proposed edit in a diff window with accept and reject buttons; the boxes on the slides are the terminal’s form of the same question.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Claude Code in RStudio’s Terminal tab
text:
Claude Code in RStudio’s Terminal tab



One RStudio window: Claude Code in the Terminal tab, the Console free for running scripts, the Files pane showing what was written. The project on screen is another one; the layout is the same.


Claude Code runs in RStudio’s Terminal tab, the tab where git commands go, opened inside the project so the folder it sees is the repository. The Console stays free, so the script it writes runs where scripts always run: Session → Restart R, then Source. The Files pane shows what it wrote. Enlarge the Terminal pane before a prompt: drag the divider up, or use the maximize icon in the pane’s corner. An approval box for a twenty-line file does not fit the default pane.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Launching Claude Code in manual mode
text:
Launching Claude Code in manual mode
claude --permission-mode manual
One line in the Terminal tab launches it in manual mode, where it reads freely but asks before every edit and every command that changes something. Depending on the plan, a session may otherwise start in auto mode, where a second model reviews actions instead of you. The status line above the prompt says which mode you are in; it must read ⏸ manual mode on for everything today. Shift+Tab cycles the modes; if the keystroke does not reach the tool inside RStudio’s terminal, quit with /exit and relaunch with the line above. The mode’s configuration name is default, so --permission-mode default launches the same mode.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents

The trust question



The trust question. Read the path; the highlighted answer is No, exit. The screen is from another folder; yours ends in placements.


The first launch in a folder asks whether you trust it. The highlighted answer is No, exit. Press the down arrow once to Yes, I trust this folder, then Enter. It asks once per folder. title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Reading the welcome screen



The welcome screen, with the empty middle of the terminal cut out. The captured account is not a student account; on your laptop the second line names your plan and its model, in wording that varies.


Four lines matter: the version; the model and plan (yours differ from the captured account’s); the folder; and the status line, ⏸ manual mode on. The folder must end in placements (on Windows it starts with C:/Users/); the captured screen shows another folder. The ❯ is where a prompt goes; Enter sends it.
Every Claude Code screen on this page comes from real runs, captured in September 2026 with the version the welcome screen shows; the RStudio screens are separate captures. The interface changes between versions, and replies vary from run to run: the wording of a summary, sometimes the code. The steps do not.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: One task per prompt: the four parts
text:
One task per prompt: the four parts

The goal: what the script must do, with names for its inputs and its output.
The mistake to avoid, named: the plausible wrong reading. Call it the failure mode.
The file to write, and where: code/<name>.R.
What not to do: no other files; no git, so that you read the diff and commit; and whether to run the script.
Prompt 1 had three of the four; Prompt 2, the scraper, has all four. Paste them; do not retype them.

A prompt that hands the tool one task has four parts, in any order. The goal: what the script must do, with names for what it reads and what it writes. The mistake to avoid, named: the plausible wrong reading a careful person could take; call it the failure mode. The file to write and where: which file, in which folder. What not to do: no other files; no git, so that the commit stays yours and the diff gets read; and whether to run the script or leave that to you. The fourth part is what keeps the diff small enough to read. Prompt 1 had a goal, a file and a “what not to do”; Prompt 2, the scraper, has all four. Every prompt on this page is the exact text of the captured run; paste it, do not retype it.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: How much to ask for in one prompt: one task, one file
text:
How much to ask for in one prompt: one task, one file







Too big to check
Right-sized




“Do my analysis of the placements.”
“Write code/placements.R: the table on the placements page, saved as data/placements.csv, four columns.”


“Make a report on placements.”
“Add a column postdoc: TRUE when the position is a postdoc. Change nothing else.”


“Fix my script.”
“The 2015 rows are missing; change the line that filters the years, nothing else.”



“Do my analysis of the placements” cannot be checked, because no number in the answer is one you could have worked out first. “Write code/placements.R: the table at that address saved as data/placements.csv” can: the page shows 16 rows for 2026, you count them in a few seconds, and the CSV must contain 16 rows for 2026 or the script is wrong. “Add a column postdoc” can too: the browser’s find box counts the spellings on the page.
So the unit to hand over is one task that writes one file and produces at least one number you can get yourself. A large job is several of these in a row, each checked before the next is sent, one per conversation. That is also why the third row of the table replaces “Fix my script” with a sentence naming the one thing that is wrong: it turns an open-ended request into a change whose size you know before you read the diff.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Three questions before you send a prompt
text:
Three questions before you send a prompt

Can you say in advance what a wrong answer would look like, and write that into the prompt?
Can you work out one number of the answer yourself, from the page or from rows on your screen?
Could you read the whole diff in five minutes?


Any no: the task is too big. Split it and send the first part.

Before pasting, three questions, and all three are about what you will do after the reply arrives.
Can you say in advance what a wrong answer would look like? Not “might it be wrong”, but what shape the error would take: rows dropped by a bad match, the countries averaged instead of the people, the other table on the page read instead of this one. You write that sentence into the prompt, which is the “mistake to avoid” part of the four. If no wrong answer occurs to you, you do not yet understand the task well enough to check it.
Can you work out one number of the answer yourself? One number is enough, from the page or from rows on your screen: 16 rows for the most recent year, 25 postdocs, two countries in Oceania. You get it before the script runs, so that the comparison afterwards is a comparison and not an impression.
Could you read the whole diff in five minutes? One new file of thirty lines, yes. Four files and two hundred lines, no: you will skim, and skimming is how a wrong line gets committed.
A no to any of them means the task is too big. Split it and send the first part; the next parts get easier to check once the first is in.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
The five-step delegation loop



The five-step delegation loop. When the value on paper and the printed value disagree, the arrow goes back to step 2 as a patch request.


Every delegation runs the same five steps. State the goal and the mistake you do not want (the failure mode). Delegate one task. Count by hand what it must return on a case small enough to check, on the page or from rows you can see, before anything runs. Run it and compare the printed value with the one on paper; if they disagree, read the diff, ask for a patch, run again. Then write the hand check into the script as a line that stops it when the value drifts (stopifnot()), so the next run checks itself. The value on paper comes from the data, not from a guess; that is what makes step 4 a comparison and not an impression.
This loop wraps the loop inside the tool. The tool gathers context, acts and checks its own result; you decide what right means and check it once more from outside. Anthropic’s best practices for Claude Code give the same advice in their own words: state verification criteria in the prompt (an example input and its expected output), scope the task to one file and one scenario, describe the symptom and what fixed looks like when asking for a fix, and, in the list of common failures, “If you can’t verify it, don’t ship it.” The five steps are that advice arranged for a novice who runs the script and reads the diff in person.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Prompt 2: the scraper, run until it works
text:
Prompt 2: the scraper, run until it works


Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)

Write code/placements.R. It reads the table "Recent job placements" at
https://business.cornell.edu/admissions/graduate/phd-aem/for-hire/ and saves
it as data/placements.csv with the page's four columns, year, name, position,
organization, one row per graduate. Use the rvest package for the HTML and
base R for the rest. Run it with Rscript code/placements.R; if it fails, fix
the script and run again. Then show me the first five rows and the number of
rows. Do not use git.

The prompt has the four parts: the goal with names, the file and its path, what not to do, and one more sentence than before: run it, and fix it if it fails.
Two of those need a word. “Run it with Rscript” is new: until now every prompt on this page left the running to you, and this one hands it over, because the check that follows is yours either way. “Do not use git” looks like a contradiction one slide after asking the tool to initialize the repository, and it is the opposite: a commit the tool makes for you is a diff you never read. Prompt 1 was the exception, and even there the exact git command appeared in a box before it ran. From here the tool writes and runs; you read the diff and commit. That sentence is repeated in the next two prompts, and then it disappears into CLAUDE.md, which says it once for every prompt after that. In the captured run the tool first ran two short R commands to look at the page (the page has two tables, one for alumni for hire and one for placements), then wrote the script, ran it, and reported: 109 rows, the first five, and how it chose the table. It ran cleanly the first time; a scraper often does not, and the sentence “if it fails, fix the script and run again” is what lets the tool iterate without you.
The check is yours. The total, 109, is too long to count by hand, so count one year: the 2026 rows sit at the top of the table, sixteen of them when captured. In the Console, sum(read.csv("data/placements.csv")$year == 2026) must print the same number. If it does not, the scraper dropped or duplicated rows, which is exactly the silent error a clean run hides.






TipThe captured transcript





⏺ Reply:
  Let me look at the page structure first.

cat("n tables:", length(tbls), "\n")

hs <- html_elements(pg, "h2, h3, h4"); print(html_text2(hs))
')

section: The approval box for a new file
text:
The approval box for a new file



The approval box for a new file. The whole file is on screen before it exists. The screen is from another project; the box is the same.


In manual mode the tool shows the file before it exists. The box names the action (Create file), the path, every line of the file, and a question with three answers. 1. Yes (Enter) writes the file. 2. Yes, and switch to accept edits turns the edit questions off for the session; leave it today. 3. No, or Esc, refuses and lets you say why. For the scraper, the lines to read before pressing anything are the ones that pick the table; the next section shows them.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: git diff --staged on the scraper: the lines to read
text:
git diff --staged on the scraper: the lines to read
git add code/placements.R
git diff --staged
wanted  <- c("year", "name", "position", "organization")
headers <- lapply(tables, function(tb) tolower(html_text2(html_elements(tb, "th"))))
hit     <- which(vapply(headers, function(h) identical(h, wanted), logical(1)))
if (length(hit) != 1) {
  stop("Expected exactly one placements table with columns ", ...)
}
A new file has no earlier version, so git diff alone shows nothing; git add it, then git diff --staged prints every line with a +. That is the whole of what the tool did. Read it once from the top. In VS Code, the Source Control view shows the same new file with every line green; reading it there and reading it in the terminal are the same act. The lines above are the ones that carry the risk: they collect every table on the page, keep the one whose header is exactly the four names, and stop the script if there is not exactly one such table. A future change to the page fails loudly instead of writing the wrong table.
Three functions a novice may not know, and may ask the tool to explain or replace: html_elements() finds every element of a kind on the page; vapply() applies a function to each table and promises a logical result; identical() compares two vectors as a whole. “Explain vapply on line 19, then rewrite it as a for loop if that is clearer” is a fair prompt. title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: How to judge a model’s diff: five questions
text:
How to judge a model’s diff: five questions

Which files changed? Only the ones you named? (git status)
What was deleted? Read the red lines first. Did you ask for each one to go?
Which line does the actual work? Does it do what you asked, and nothing more?
Where does each value in it come from? Your data, or typed into the code by the tool?
Is there a line you could not explain to someone? Ask what it does before you accept it.

Five questions, in order, every time, whether the diff is in the approval box or in git diff. Are the only changed files the ones you named (git status)? Are there - lines, and did you ask for each removal? Which line does the math, and does it match the failure mode you named? For every value the new lines contain, can you say where it came from: your data, your prompt, or the tool’s own knowledge? Is there a line you cannot explain? For the last one, ask for an explanation before accepting, or ask for a version that uses only functions you know. Read the deletions first: a line removed without being asked for is the dangerous kind. Question 4 is the one worth slowing down on: a value that came neither from your data nor from your prompt came from the tool’s memory, and memory is not a source. The country column, later today, is where these five questions earn their keep.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Prompt 3: a postdoc flag


Prompt to paste into Claude Code (captured run)

Add a column postdoc to the table before it is saved: TRUE when the position
is a postdoc, FALSE otherwise. Change nothing else. Run it again and tell me
how many rows are TRUE.

+# Flag postdoc positions; spellings on the page include "Postdoc", "Post-doc",
+# "Post Doctoral Fellow" and "Postdoctoral Associate".
+placements$postdoc <- grepl("post[- ]?doc", placements$position, ignore.case = TRUE)
A one-line task with a check you can do in the browser. The tool first printed every position containing “post”, eleven spellings from “Post-doc” to “Earth Institute Postdoctoral Fellow”, then added one comment and one line: a pattern that accepts “postdoc”, “post-doc” and “post doc” in any case. It ran the script again and reported 25 of 109 rows TRUE, and flagged one judgment call, a graduate listed as “Postdoctoral Associate; Assistant Professor of Economics”, counted as TRUE.
The hand check is the browser’s find box on the page. Find is not case-sensitive, so “postdoc” counts every “Postdoc” and “Postdoctoral”, 15 when captured; “post-doc” counts the hyphenated ones, 9; “post doc” counts the one with a space. 25. A pattern that matched only “postdoc” would have printed 15 and run clean; that is the failure mode this check catches, and it is worth trying on purpose in the practice set.

section: The approval box for an edit: red and green lines
text:
The approval box for an edit: red and green lines



The approval box for an edit. Two red lines: the line asked about, and a header comment rewritten without being asked. The screen is from another project; the box is the same.


The tool shows an edit as a diff before it lands: removed lines in red with -, added lines in green with +. Read every red line first. In the box shown, two lines go: the line asked about, and a header comment the tool rewrote although nobody asked. It is harmless, and it is the kind of extra change the red lines exist to show. 1. Yes accepts. The postdoc edit is one comment and one line, all green; the country edit is thirty green lines, and every country name in them is question 4. Editor extensions show the same edit in a diff window with accept and reject buttons; whichever window you read it in, the diff is the same object git diff prints.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
section: Your own check, typed into the script and committed with it
text:
Your own check, typed into the script and committed with it
 placements$postdoc <- grepl("post[- ]?doc", placements$position, ignore.case = TRUE)
+
+# Counted on the page on 2026-09-21: 16 rows for 2026; postdoc spellings
+# 15 + 9 + 1. When the page changes this stops the script: recount, then edit.
+stopifnot(sum(placements$year == 2026) == 16, sum(placements$postdoc) == 25)
You counted two things yourself: 16 rows for the most recent year, on the page, and 25 postdocs, with the browser’s find box. So far those counts live in your head and on a scrap of paper, and they check the script once. One line turns them into a check the script makes every time anyone runs it. stopifnot() does nothing when its conditions are true and stops the script, naming the condition, when one is false.
Type it yourself in RStudio, after the postdoc line and before write.csv, save, then Session → Restart R and Source: no error, which means the script reproduced both of your numbers. Type it rather than asking the tool for it: the checker should not be the thing being checked. Then commit the script, check and all. From that commit on, the check is part of the code: it travels with the file, it runs for whoever opens the project next, and it is in the history with your name on it.
The counts will go stale: the page adds a class every year. When it does, the script stops with Error: sum(placements$year == 2026) == 16 is not TRUE, which is the script telling you that the source changed and the counts need redoing. Recount on the page, edit the numbers and the date in the comment, run again. A check that never fails is a check on nothing.
The commit message says who wrote what: the scraper and the flag came from the tool, the counts are yours. That one sentence is also what fills the disclosure block of a submission.
git add code/placements.R
git commit -m "Scrape placements, flag postdocs (Claude Code); two hand counts"
git log --oneline
#> <your hash> Scrape placements, flag postdocs (Claude Code); two hand counts
#> <your hash> New project

The diff for the country column: where does each value come from?
country_patterns <- c(
  "Australia"    = "Monash|New South Wales|University of Sydney",
  "Canada"       = "Alberta|Calgary|Ottawa",

Question 4 of the five, asked of this diff: for each value the new column can take, where did it come from? The organization column comes from the page, and the code matches fragments of it. But every country name in the result is typed into the script: sixteen of them in the table, and "United States" as the value every row starts with and keeps if no pattern matches it, which is 77 of the 109 rows.
So the column is not read from anywhere. It is produced by the tool’s own knowledge of these institutions, written into your code as if it were data. The next section counts how much of it the page can support.

title: 9 · AI II — coding agents
text:
Where the countries came from

The page names a place for 14 of 109 rows. Nothing else on the page says a country.
The rest is memory: a table it typed, and a default. It said so, in a comment and in its reply, and the column still went into the CSV.
DTUM: Denmark in one run, Germany in the next. Same prompt, same page.
Plausible is not the same as right. A fact it did not read is a guess, however confident the sentence around it.
The script ran without error both times.

Count what the page supports. Fourteen of the 109 organization strings name a place (“University of Alberta, Canada”, “KDI School … (Korea)”, “Federal Home Loan Bank of Topeka, KS”). For the other 95 the page says nothing, and the tool cannot read a country from a name; it can only remember one. The table it typed is a set of claims about the world, and the default is a larger one: 77 rows became “United States” because no pattern matched them, which is the same fate for “Clarkson University” and for an organization it had never heard of.
The tool was honest about it. The comment says “inferred”, the reply says the page has no country field, and it flagged the two entries it was least sure of. Honesty in the transcript does not change what is in the CSV: a country column with no source, ready to be mapped, tabulated and cited.
Run the same prompt twice and the guess moves. On the same evening, the first run read “DTUM” as DTU Management in Denmark; the second, from the same page with the same prompt, read it as the Technical University of Munich in Germany. Both runs wrote a country, both ran without error, and both replies said the assignments looked right. That is what “plausible is not the same as right” looks like in a column.

section: What would have caught it earlier
text:
What would have caught it earlier

A plan before code. “Describe your approach before writing any code.” The captured reply proposes a lookup table it would “populate myself from knowledge of the institutions” and mark “the handful I’m unsure about”. You read that and say no.
Question 4 of the five, asked of the diff. Where does each value come from? Sixteen country names sit in the code, and none of them came from the page or from you.
A reviewer with fresh eyes. A second Claude that never saw this conversation, later today, found it in one turn.

Three habits from the first part of this page would each have caught the column before it existed. The cheapest is the plan. Sent on the same project before Prompt 4, “Describe your approach before writing any code” produced the reply below: a hand-curated lookup table, filled in “from knowledge of the institutions”, with the uncertain ones flagged. A reader who owns the question stops there: the source is the model’s memory, so the column is not wanted in that form.
The second is question 4 of the five questions for any diff: are the where does each value come from? Sixteen country names and a default sit in the code itself. None came from the page, and none came from your prompt. The third is a reviewer that never saw the conversation, the subagent in the seventh part of this page, which reported the table and the default with line numbers in one turn.






TipThe captured plan reply, in full





⏺ Reply:
  Here's what I found and what I'd do.
  
  **What's there.** `code/placements.R` scrapes the Dyson placements table and writes `data/placements.csv` (109 rows; columns `year, name, position, organization, postdoc`). The `organization` column has ~105 distinct free-text strings — mixed granularity (`"Brown"`, `"NUS"`, `"DTUM"`, `"Stout"`), embedded departments (`"Purdue University, Department of Agricultural Economics"`), occasional location hints (`"Peking University (Beijing)"`, `"KDI School … (Korea)"`, `"University of Alberta, Canada"`), and a few two-organization entries (`"National Bureau of Economic Research, Claremont McKenna College"`).
  
  **Approach: a hand-curated lookup table, joined in the script.**
  
  1. **New file `data/org_country.csv`** with two columns, `organization, country`, one row per distinct organization string exactly as it appears in the scraped data (after `trimws`). I'd populate it myself from knowledge of the institutions, and mark the handful I'm unsure about in my reply so you can check them.
  2. **Edit `code/placements.R`**: after the `postdoc` flag and before `write.csv`, read the lookup, `match()` on the exact organization string, and add `placements$country`. If any organization isn't in the table, print the unmapped names and leave `country = NA` (warn rather than stop, so a re-scrape never fails when a new graduate appears — you just extend the table). Column order: `year, name, position, organization, country, postdoc`.
  
  **Why a lookup table rather than the alternatives.**
  - Regex heuristics ("University of X" → US) break immediately on `University of Sydney`, `University of Bern`, `University of Calgary`.
  - Geocoding / ROR / web APIs add a network dependency and choke on abbreviations like `NUS`, `IIMA`, `DTUM`, `Brown`.
  - The dataset is ~100 rows; a table is trivial to maintain, fully reproducible, and the script rewrites `placements.csv` on every run, so the mapping has to live outside that file anyway.
  
  **Judgment calls I'd make unless you say otherwise.**
  - **Country labels:** plain English short names (`United States`, `United Kingdom`, `South Korea`, `Hong Kong`, …). I can add an ISO3 code column too if you want it for later joins.
  - **International organizations** (World Bank, IMF, Inter-American Development Bank, USAID): `United States` — headquarters location. Alternative is a separate "International" label; say which you prefer.
  - **Hong Kong**: `Hong Kong`, not `China`.
  - **Multinationals** (Uber, Citibank, Morgan Stanley, Capital One, StoneX, Acadian): country of headquarters (US), since the `position` text doesn't give an office location.
  - **Two-org entries**: country of the first-listed organization (both examples are US anyway).
  - **Uncertain ones I'd flag:** `DTUM` (likely DTU Management, Denmark), `Stout` (US consulting firm), `Cooper/Smith` (US), `Econic Partners LLC` (US), `Center for Governmental Research` (US, Rochester NY).
  
  If that all sounds right — or you want ISO codes / a different rule for international orgs — tell me and I'll write it.

Filling the file is research, not typing: each country comes from the organization’s own page, and a row you cannot settle stays empty. Commit the file with a message that says the countries are yours.
